news.title: 'I'm about to go kill this kid': The frantic 911 call made by Oregon school shooting hero
news.text:
The man who fatally shot a teenager who killed a teacher and three students at an Oregon elementary school told a 911 operator “I’m about to go kill this kid,” it has emerged.

Kaylub Giamanco has been hailed as a hero for intervening during the deadly rampage at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend in October.

The 36-year-old, a local carpenter, was driving home to eat lunch when he saw a teen, dressed in black, firing a shotgun at a pickup truck and scaling the perimeter fence to the school.

The teen was later identified as 16-year-old Griffin J. John II.

Giamanco retrieved a .40-caliber handgun from his truck console, loaded a magazine and called 911 before heading onto the property.

The tense call, lasting a little more than a minute, was released Tuesday.

In it, Giamanco told the 911 operator that there was “someone with a gun” at the school that his daughter attended.

“I have a gun and I will shoot them right now,” he said.

The operator told him: “Don’t do anything, let me get an officer there.” 

They then talked over each other, with Giamanco sounding increasingly frustrated.

“I’m about to go kill this kid,” he told the 911 operator.

A few seconds later, he said that the shooter was entering the building. The operator asked if the shooter was firing, and Giamanco said yes.

The operator tried to get more information, but the call ended.

The teen had shot his way through locked doors to get into the elementary school, killing three children and a teacher in a special needs classroom.

Another student was critically injured and a teacher was injured and hospitalized.

Giamanco earlier told Oregon Public Broadcasting that he heard children “pleading for their lives” when he entered the building.

“I started hearing gunfire and I just started army crawling faster and faster, and I told myself this is probably the last thing that I’m ever going to do.”

He fired at the gunman once and he dropped to the floor, but discharged two additional rounds when the gunman reached for his weapon again.

“He was scrambling for his weapon,” Giamanco said. “I looked at him and I shot him two more times to make sure that he couldn’t move because I was afraid of him shooting anybody else.”

Police have said that Giamanco’s actions prevented further loss of life at the 400-student campus, and President Donald Trump praised him as “a great hero that went in and did the business.”

However, he earlier said that he was overcome with grief for the students that he could not protect.

“I want to apologize for not saving their babies,” Giamanco told OPB. “The gratitude for saving people’s children is awesome, but there were ones that I didn’t save.”
news.summary: Kaylub Giamanco told a 911 operator ‘I have a gun and I will shoot them right now’
news.author: Martha Bellisle

news.title: US Midterm Elections 2026: Some Voters Disrupted By Weather, Machine Issues
news.text: The final day of voting in this year's midterm elections arrived Tuesday against a backdrop of uncertainty after a year in which President Donald Trump has tried to interfere in how states run their elections and sown doubts about the outcome should Republicans lose.Millions of Americans already cast their ballots, with early voting turnout on pace to eclipse that of the last midterm elections. In contrast to the president's continued rhetoric about election cheating, voting so far has unfolded with relatively few problems.By afternoon on Election Day, the biggest issues affecting voting were weather-related, with flooding in Florida and parts of the Southwest prompting changes to polling locations and other emergency measures. A problem with ballot scanners also was delaying vote counting — though voting was able to continue — in New York's suburban Westchester County, part of which is in a U.S. House district with a competitive race.Trump has spent months trying to use the power of the presidency to put his thumb on the scale of this year's elections, which will determine whether his party keeps control of Congress.His Justice and Homeland Security departments have been involved in a massive hunt for voters who are not U.S. citizens, at one point engaging in a made-for-the-cameras predawn operation that led to more than two dozen arrests in California. The Department of Justice was making its largest-ever effort to monitor Election Day polling places across all 50 states, countered by an even larger effort among Democrats and allied groups, and at the president's urging had sued to block certification of Alaska's results if the outcome of the Senate race favored Democrats. A federal judge on Sunday dismissed that lawsuit.At the same time, Trump's constant false claims about widespread voter fraud led election officials and Democratic groups across the country to plan for the possibility of immigration agents at voting sites or federal officers seizing voting machines. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement posted a warning on its X account Tuesday that pushed the administration's narrative about noncitizen voting: “We will track you down, arrest you, and prosecute you,” the post read. “There will be no escape.”The agency did not immediately return a request for comment about the post. The Trump administration has insisted that no armed federal officials would be guarding the polls on Election Day, and on Tuesday, none of the steps Democrats most feared had yet come to pass.Polling sites were open Tuesday across much of the country, with few disruptions so far.Hannah Fried, co-founder and CEO of the voting rights group All Voting Is Local, said the limited issues she was seeing so far at polling places were “garden-variety stuff that any of us who works on elections is used to seeing, and it's quickly resolved.”In Westchester County, election officials said ballot scanners were not accepting paper ballots, an issue that resulted from a program update made after polling equipment was initially prepared and tested. That required the ballots to be placed in emergency bags for later counting. Election officials stressed that the ballots would remain secure and monitored and that voters could continue casting ballots while they worked to resolve the issue.One resident, registered Democrat Benjamin Hort, said he opted not to cast a provisional ballot Tuesday and plans to come back later in the day, when he hoped the machines would be operational.“I'll wait as long as I have to,” Hort said. “You would think they would have tested the machines. Not ideal.”Westchester County Executive Ken Jenkins vowed to launch a bipartisan investigation into what he called a “debacle.”At polling locations across Florida's Broward County, voting was delayed for 20 minutes after polls opened because a new voting system safety feature malfunctioned, officials said. Supervisor of Elections Joe Scott apologized to voters who had to wait, and said some left before they were able to vote. The problem was solved by 7:20 a.m., and Scott encouraged those who left to return. He did not have an estimate for how many people left.Heavy rains and flash flooding in a swath of the Southwest were making it harder for some voters to reach polling places in parts of Colorado, Arizona, Utah and New Mexico. Election administrators in the Navajo Nation announced changes to several of its polling locations, and in Utah's rural San Juan County, voters were being allowed to vote electronically on Tuesday because some of them may not be able to get to polling places.Flooding in eight Florida counties also prompted some last-minute polling location changes in the state. Amy Keith, the Florida state director for Common Cause, said the flooding is a big issue.“Today it has already been a pretty challenging morning,” she said, urging voters to double check their voting locations with election supervisors.Election administrators and voting rights advocates had advised voters casting late absentee ballots to use drop boxes or deliver them to polling places in person rather than mail them. The advice came after concerns emerged that recent changes in U.S. Postal Service operations could result in postmarking delays that would mean mail ballots could not be counted. Late-arriving ballots or late postmarks disenfranchised tens of thousands of voters during this year's primaries in California, Oregon and Washington, which mail ballots to all voters.The Republican administration's legal maneuvers have been largely blocked by the courts.One of the Trump administration's most high-profile attempts to interfere in state elections was turned away Monday night by the U.S. Supreme Court, which rejected its push to force California to set aside thousands of ballots as part of its search for noncitizen voters. In another Monday night ruling, a federal judge said the Trump administration must stop sending voter lists of alleged noncitizens to election officials.Even the administration's own record of arrests and charges has demonstrated what research and state investigations have made clear for years — that instances of noncitizens casting ballots are extremely rare.The president faced another defeat in the Supreme Court less than two months ago, when it rejected his attempt to limit mail balloting through changes at the Postal Service. That directive was included in one of two executive orders Trump has signed during his second term that attempted to federalize certain aspects of elections, even though the Constitution gives the states, and sometimes Congress, the authority to set election rules.Voting rights groups, Democrats and the Justice Department have been exchanging a flurry of legal filings that reveal how Trump's attempts to expand federal control over state-run elections — combined with high-stakes races — are resulting in court battles that could extend past Election Day into ballot counting and certification of the results.Election law experts said Trump's lawsuits go beyond historic norms, but that the administration's legal arguments were unlikely to convince judges.Trump also has ramped up his own equivocations about whether the election will be legitimate, as he has in the past. A week before Election Day, when a reporter asked him if he would accept the results, he offered a qualified answer.“I will if they are honest,” he said.
news.summary: US Midterm Elections 2026: Millions of Americans already cast their ballots, with early voting turnout on pace to eclipse that of the last midterm elections. In contrast to the president's continued rhetoric about election cheating, voting so far has unfolded with relatively few problems.
news.author: Associated Press

news.title: Swastikas Painted on Jewish School Buses in New York
news.text: Swastikas and “anti-Semitic writing” were allegedly spraypainted onto four school buses that serve orthodox Jewish schools in New York. Photos posted on Monday by the Williamsburg News show the Nazi symbols painted in black on what the outlet reported was four separate buses. Other phrases included “USA First,” “f**k Israel” and “Free Palestine.” The New York City Police Department (NYPD) told Newsweek that its Hate Crime Task Force is investigating following a 911 call on Monday morning. The alleged “criminal mischief” took place “in the vicinity of Bedford Avenue and Williamsburg Street, within the confines of the 90 Precinct,” the NYPD said. No arrests had been made as of mid-afternoon Tuesday. Williamsburg is home to a large Jewish community—an estimated 36,000 Jewish adults and 32,000 children as of 2023, according to a UJA-Federation of New York’s Jewish Community Study. The buses serve the Satmar, Sanz-Klausenburg and Tiferes Yisrael Jewish communities, according to Williamsburg 365—these are Orthodox Jewish religious sects whose institutions include schools. None of them have spoken out publicly. Newsweek has reached out to offices for the United Talmudical Academy, the Sanz-Klausenburg Congregation in Williamsburg and Talmud Torah Tiferes Yisroel. Multiple New York City officials have spoken out against the vandalism, including Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who called it “abhorrent.” Phylisa Wisdom, who leads the mayor’s Office to Combat Antisemitism, told Newsweek that the city would “use every tool at our disposal” to find those responsible. It comes amid growing concern about a rise in antisemitism in New York and around the U.S. NYPD figures show 245 confirmed anti-Jewish hate crimes in the first nine months of 2026, up from 242 in the same period last year and accounting for approximately 53 percent of all confirmed hate crimes citywide. Last year was the third-highest year on record for antisemitic incidents recorded by the Jewish advocacy organization Anti-Defamation League (ADL) with 6,274. That was down from a peak of 9,354 in 2024 and 8,873 in 2023, following seven years of the figures fluctuating between 1,000 and 3,000. The FBI, whose data covers hate crimes reported by law enforcement rather than the ADL’s broader range of incidents, recorded 1,648 anti-Jewish hate-crime incidents across America in 2025 and 1,030 so far this year. New York Officials Respond New York Attorney General Letitia James called the acts “despicable” in a post on X, urging anyone with information to contact law enforcement. “Antisemitism and hate have no home in New York,” she said. Governor Kathy Hochul called for those responsible to be “prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.” “As a mother and grandmother, it sickens me to think of children arriving at school to find their buses defaced with swastikas and hateful antisemitic messages,” she wrote on X. “No Jewish child or family should have to endure this kind of fear and intimidation.” Mamdani, a progressive Democrat who has repeatedly criticized Israel, spoke out about the "antisemitic vandalism" in Williamsburg in a post on X. “Every New Yorker — especially our children — deserves to live free of such hatred,” he said. “We will continue to use every tool at our disposal to confront antisemitism, hold those responsible accountable and ensure that hatred has no place in our city.” Newsweek was directed to the post when it contacted Mamdani's office. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu previously accused Mamdani of endangering Jewish New Yorkers with his rhetoric about Israel during a September speech at the United Nations. It came after Mamdani, who has repeatedly rejected accusations of antisemitism, announced a detailed strategy to fight antisemitism, promising to “build a city where Jewish New Yorkers are not only safe but celebrated.” He pledged millions in a plan that includes funding for synagogues, an increased focus on folding Jewish history into public school education, and a pledge to highlight important Jewish cultural and religious sites. The plan has since faced criticism from Israeli officials and local groups for not formally defining antisemitism and failing to confront whether anti-Israel rhetoric can have a role in it. Rabbi Rick Jacobs, president of the Union for Reform Judaism, praised the strategy but called on Mamdani to address "anti-Israel rhetoric that makes Jewish New Yorkers vulnerable as there are clearly times when antisemitic attacks are fueled by anti-Zionism." Addressing questions about it at the time, Mamdani told reporters: "When it comes to criticism of the Israeli prime minister or the Israeli government, that has no bearing on our responsibility to keep Jewish New Yorkers safe. "And also, to say very clearly, that the responsibility for the Israeli government's actions lies with the Israeli government. It does not lie with Jewish New Yorkers." The Backdrop All three sources for antisemitic incidents in the U.S. reviewed by Newsweek recorded a spike after October 7, 2023, when Hamas militants attacked Israel, killing roughly 1,200 people and abducting 251 to the Gaza Strip. Israel has since killed 74,615 people in the Gaza Strip as of Tuesday, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry, which does not differentiate between civilian and militant deaths. Many pro-Palestine activists stress that their criticism is directed against Israel as a state, not Jewish people, but there are others who use anger over the war to justify antisemitism. Debate over the distinction between criticism of Israel and antisemitism, and what constitutes which, has featured prominently in America’s political climate in the last three years, fueling, not exclusively but significantly, major rifts in both parties. President Donald Trump has faced a huge divide among his supporters over his backing for Israel, usually from conservatives aligned with his "America First" movement. That includes big names who were once seen as loyalists—like podcasters Tucker Carlson and Candace Owens, who frequently blast the Trump administration’s foreign policy as being beholden to Israel. Trump has pushed back, calling Carlson, Owens and other former supporters who turned against him "troublemakers" and "nut jobs." On Tuesday, Trump announced that the U.S. will stop sending funding packages to Israel by the end of this year after making a deal with Netanyahu. The U.S. currently provides Israel with roughly $3.8 billion in military aid each year, but the memorandum of understanding signed under former President Barack Obama outlining this commitment is due to lapse in 2028. Meanwhile, in the Democratic Party, disagreements over Israel and antisemitism often play out as part of a wider split between the party’s progressives and moderates. In a recent example in Michigan, Democratic Representative Haley Stevens withdrew her support for the party’s Senate candidate, Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive she endorsed after he defeated her in the primary, and backed Republican Mike Rogers on Sunday. Stevens, a staunch Israel supporter, cited the issue as a significant reason for her decision to reverse course on El-Sayed, a fierce critic of the U.S. ally. While the current backdrop for the debate centers on the war in the Middle East, Washington’s relationship with Israel and concerns about free speech and antisemitism predates the modern state of Israel, and the contemporary discussions about what defines it, by centuries. The U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum says it is “based on old and widespread prejudices” that culminated in the Holocaust, when Nazi Germany murdered 6 million European Jews. But it adds: "Antisemitism did not begin or end with the Holocaust, antisemitism has existed for thousands of years." Contact Newsweek editors on this story: John Fitzpatrick and Dave Siminoff.
news.summary: The NYPD's Hate Crime Task Force is investigating the vandalism in Williamsburg.
news.author: Jordan King

news.title: Bruce Springsteen Urges Officials to Protect the Vote on Election Day: ‘Our Vote Is Our Voice’
news.text:
Skip to main content

Bruce Springsteen performs at the AFI FEST 2025 Presented By Canva Opening Night "Springsteen: Deliver Me From Nowhere" Premiere at TCL Chinese Theatre on October 22, 2025 in Hollywood, California.

Rodin Eckenroth/Getty Images for AFI

Bruce Springsteen has a message for election officials on Election Day.

On Tuesday (Nov. 3), the 77-year-old music icon and longtime political activist shared a brief video message on social media, urging “election officials and representatives of our government” to ensure votes are securely counted.

Bruce Springsteen Has No Regrets About His Political Tour: ‘I Do What I Want to Do’

Bruce Springsteen Slams ICE at New Jersey Benefit Show: ‘Get the F—k Out of Minneapolis’

Bruce Springsteen Backs Michigan’s Dr. Abdul El-Sayed for U.S. Senate Amid Haley Stevens Reversal: ‘He’s a Fighter’

Standing in front of a stone wall and dressed in a flannel shirt, Springsteen delivered a direct appeal to those overseeing the electoral process.

“I’m speaking to election officials and representatives of our government on Election Day,” Springsteen said on Instagram. “You have sworn an oath to preserve, protect, and defend our Constitution. That means you have a solemn duty to ensure that our votes are securely counted.”

He continued, “Thomas Jefferson said, ‘Government requires a consent of the governed.’ You who represent us must never consent to any directives that undermine our constitutional right to a free and fair election.”

Election Day marks the 2026 midterm elections, with voters across the country casting ballots in congressional races that will determine control of the House of Representatives and Senate. Voters are also deciding a number of gubernatorial, state legislative and local contests.

“Our vote is our voice,” Springsteen said in conclusion. “And it’s up to you to ensure that our voice is heard. I wish you all a good Election Day, and thank you for your service.”

In the caption accompanying the 45-second clip, Springsteen thanked those voting on Election Day and encouraged his followers to continue supporting democracy by taking the Oath to the Constitution at oathproject.org.

Merck Mercuriadis, founder of the influential music catalog investment group Hipgnosis, took to the comments, writing, “The boss has spoken – for 50 years he has spoken truthfully about the cracks in ‘merica in order to help us become the best version of ourselves that we can be. Born to vote!!!!!!!!!”

This isn’t the first time Springsteen has spoken out about voting rights and election integrity. In 2012, the “Dancing in the Dark” singer-songwriter criticized voter suppression efforts in several states, writing that Americans of all political views should oppose what he described as “anti-voter, anti-citizen efforts.” He also raised concerns about the future of American democracy during the 2024 presidential election, when he endorsed Kamala Harris and Tim Walz.

A vocal critic of President Donald Trump and longtime Democratic supporter, Springsteen released his protest anthem “Streets of Minneapolis” earlier this year in response to the fatal shootings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti amid the administration’s immigration crackdown. He also performed the song during his recent Land of Hope and Dreams Tour.

During a January 2026 benefit concert in New Jersey, Springsteen also spoke out about the Trump administration, saying, “The United States, the ideals and the values for which it stood for the past 250 years, is being tested like it has never been in modern times. Those values and those ideals have never been as endangered as they are right now.”

On Monday (Nov. 2), Springsteen also threw his support behind Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in the Michigan Senate race.

“Dr. El-Sayed is a fighter for our American Constitution, he’s a fighter for our American Democracy, and he’s a fighter against the corrupt, lawless, and anti-American leadership currently in the White House,” he wrote on Instagram. “That’s why I’m in his corner 100%.”

news.title: Russia and Ukraine Trade Strikes on Power Facilities and Oil Refineries
news.text:
Russian and Ukrainian forces traded attacks targeting each other’s power facilities on Nov. 3, ahead of peace talks planned for next week.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported Russian drone and missile strikes had targeted power-generation sites and substations in Odesa, Cherkasy, Zhytomyr, Vinnytsia, Kharkiv, Dnipro, Chernivtsi, Chernihiv, and Rivne.

He said the overnight Russian attack had included at least 289 attack drones, 17 ballistic missiles, and 59 cruise missiles.

“In many cities and communities, emergency and unscheduled power outages are ongoing,” Zelenskyy said.

Russia’s Ministry of Defense confirmed its forces targeted power generation facilities they assessed to be supporting Ukraine’s military.

Zelenskyy said Russian strikes on Kharkiv damaged a hospital, leaving 73 injured.

The Ukrainian leader also reported rescue operations in the Zaporizhzhia region were continuing following strikes a day earlier. He said the death toll in the region has risen to 29 people.

Citing Russia’s Ministry of Defense, the Russian state-run TASS news agency reported that 856 Ukrainian attack drones were launched overnight against multiple Russian regions and sites along the Black Sea.

Two employees were injured, and infrastructure was damaged at an oil refinery in Russia’s Yaroslavl region, TASS reported. Yaroslavl Governor Mikhail Yevrayev reported 124 drones targeted the Yaroslavl refinery.

TASS reported 493 Ukrainian drones targeted Russia’s Moscow region overnight.

Ukrainian drones were also reported over Bryansk, Belgorod, Vladimir, Kaluga, Kursk, Novgorod, Oryol, Rostov, Ryazan, Smolensk, Tver, Tula, and the Russian-held Crimean Peninsula.

Russian authorities reported that their air defense forces intercepted most of the Ukrainian attack drones.

President Donald Trump has repeatedly pressed for Russia and Ukraine to stop attacking energy sites on either side of the conflict, but to little avail.

The trilateral discussions, which would be the first since February, are aimed at advancing efforts to end the current war and determine post-conflict security arrangements.

Zelenskyy suggested Russia’s latest attacks were also deliberately timed to coincide with election day in the United States, while the U.S. general public is focused on internal politics.

“The Russians believe that America will not notice this signal from them. But such terror must be noticed and stopped,” Zelenskyy wrote.

“Ukraine must be helped to defend its skies, otherwise Russia will never stop its missile strikes. It is essential to help build peace honestly and reliably, and America can do that.”

Russian and Ukrainian forces did recently conclude a limited ceasefire around the embattled eastern Ukrainian city of Oleshky.

The ceasefire, which was brokered with the help of First Lady Melania Trump, ran from Oct. 27 to Nov. 1 and allowed the evacuation of hundreds of civilians from the area.

On Tuesday, the White House announced Melania Trump would host Russian and Ukrainian delegations at the White House on Nov. 5. She is set to deliver remarks on the recent ceasefire in Oleshky during the engagement.
news.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said several Ukrainian communities were left without power following overnight Russian attacks.
news.author: Ryan Morgan

news.title: Federal Government Begins NERSI N50,000 Cash Relief Payments to Vulnerable Nigerians
news.text:
The Minister of Humanitarian Affairs and Poverty Reduction, Dr Bernard Doro, formally announced the commencement of payments on October 30, 2026. He said eligible beneficiaries would receive N50,000 each month to help them meet essential household needs, adding that the programme would be reviewed periodically in response to changes in the cost of living.

Reports from early beneficiaries indicate that payments are flowing through three approved payment service providers at the initial stage: MoMo Payment Service Bank, ALAT by Wema Bank and NairaGram. Some recipients said they received text messages days before they noticed them, while others reported initial difficulties activating their payments before successfully completing the process and receiving credit alerts in their mobile wallets.

The payment design involves a consent step before any money moves. Eligible beneficiaries selected under NERSI receive an SMS notification from their designated payment provider, asking them to consent to the transfer. Once consent is confirmed, the N50,000 is credited to the beneficiary’s mobile wallet with the provider in question.

The Federal Government has been specific about the USSD codes that beneficiaries should use through each provider. MoMo PSB users should dial *671*0# to process their eligibility. ALAT by Wema customers can use *945*23#. NairaGram users should dial *726*00#. Beneficiaries who receive an SMS notification are advised to follow the steps provided in the genuine message from their provider, not instructions circulating on social media or received from third parties.

The programme is being implemented in phases. Beneficiaries who have not yet received a notification may receive one in a later phase, as the government releases payments in batches rather than disbursing to all eligible households at once. Accordingly, not receiving a notification in the first few days does not mean a household has been excluded from the programme.

A significant number of Nigerians have reported receiving automated messages telling them they are not currently selected to receive the relief support. This message should be read carefully. The official programme guidelines state that it does not necessarily mean permanent exclusion from the programme. Rather, it indicates that the individual is not among the current beneficiary batch. As payments are issued in phases, those who receive this message may still receive notifications in subsequent rounds.

Nigerians who are uncertain about their status or who have questions about the programme are encouraged to contact the official NERSI helpline at 0700-022-2222 for guidance. The helpline is the appropriate channel for any query about eligibility, payment timing or problems with the activation process.

Importantly, the programme is entirely free. Beneficiaries do not need to register with any agent, pay any fee or submit any application to access the funds. The Federal Government has been clear that beneficiaries are selected through verified national records, including the National Social Register, and that no external agent has any role in that process. Any individual who approaches a Nigerian claiming to be able to secure their selection or process their payment in exchange for money is operating a scam.

The Federal Government and the approved payment providers have each issued warnings about the risk of fraudulent actors exploiting the NERSI programme to defraud vulnerable citizens. Beneficiaries and non-beneficiaries alike are advised not to share their Personal Identification Numbers (PINs), One-Time Passwords (OTPs) or other banking and mobile wallet security credentials with any person or organisation, regardless of how official the request appears.

Fraudsters may attempt to impersonate NERSI officials, government ministries or the approved payment providers through phone calls, text messages or social media posts. Any contact from an unverified source that asks for security details, requests payment or offers to speed up the process should be treated with extreme suspicion. Citizens who suspect they have been targeted by fraud should report the contact to the NERSI helpline and to their payment provider’s fraud reporting line.

The government’s decision to route NERSI disbursements through established, regulated digital financial service providers is itself a fraud-mitigation measure. By channelling payments through licensed platforms that operate under Central Bank of NigeriaThe Central Bank of Nigeria, which sets interest rates and manages the naira. oversight, the programme creates an audit trail and a compliance framework that cash-based distribution methods cannot provide. It also leverages existing customer verification processes that these platforms have already conducted on their account holders.

NERSI was conceived as a direct response to the severe cost-of-living pressure bearing down on low-income Nigerian households following the removal of the fuel subsidy and the significant depreciation of the naira. The consequences of both decisions have been felt most acutely by households at the bottom of the income distribution, for whom food, transport and energy now consume a dramatically larger share of earnings than they did two years ago.

A monthly cash transfer of N50,000 will not resolve structural economic challenges, but it provides a meaningful cushion for families living on the margins. For those who receive it, the payment represents real purchasing power that can go toward food, school fees, medication or other urgent needs. The programme’s decision to use digital channels means that, in most cases, the money goes directly to the intended beneficiary rather than being intercepted along a traditional distribution chain.

Nigeria has a documented history of social protection programmes that lose significant portions of their funding to leakage, fraud and mismanagement. The digital architecture of NERSI is intended to address those weaknesses. Whether the programme delivers on that intention will become clearer as disbursements progress and independent monitoring organisations begin to assess the reach and accuracy of payments.

news.title: Embattled FIFA chief Gianni Infantino 'used Trump adviser to get work permit for his undocumented Nicaraguan housekeeper'
news.text:
FIFA President Gianni Infantino allegedly influenced Trump administration officials to fast-track a work permit for his undocumented Nicaraguan housekeeper after she lost her legal status, according to bombshell documents. 

The global soccer chief is alleged to have turned to politically-connected contacts to secure a new work permit for Yajarlin del Socorro Fernandez, 33, after the White House revoked her legal permission to work in the United States, according to documents reviewed by the Daily Mail. 

The Nicaraguan-born Fernandez was reportedly employed by the soccer governing body to work as a housekeeper for the FIFA boss and his family in August 2024. Despite being on FIFA's payroll, she performed no services for the organization. 

However, she reportedly continued illegally working in her role and living in the Infantino household for months after the Trump administration terminated the immigration agreement that granted her permission to stay in the United States.

Fernandez is then said to have secured a new work authorization under Kristi Noem's Department of Homeland Security following an intervention by a Trump adviser, documents show. 

Infantino allegedly tapped Carlos Cordeiro, the former US Soccer chief who served as a senior World Cup adviser to Donald Trump, to orchestrate the new work permit. 

In January, Infantino reportedly asked Cordeiro, who in May 2025 was appointed to the White House's World Cup task force alongside Noem, to use his connections at the state department to smooth the path to getting Fernandez's new work visa approved, according to the documents. 

Cordeiro also allegedly first helped to secure Fernandez's right to work in the US under Infantino's orders in 2024. 

Fernandez was reportedly already living and working at Infantino’s residence in the millionaires' row of One Thousand Museum in Miami, Florida, where David Beckham recently sold a $25million penthouse, in early 2024. 

However, until May 2024, she had not yet filed or received an approved work permit and was therefore working at the residence illegally, per the documents. 

During a January 2024 meeting at Infantino's home, Cordeiro, at the FIFA boss's request, is said to have instructed a subordinate to submit their own Miami rental address on Fernandez's immigration filing rather than that of the Infantino family home.

While Fernandez's work visa was initially approved, it came to an abrupt end last year when the Department of Homeland Security terminated the Humanitarian Parole Program for Cuba, Haiti, Venezuela and her native Nicaragua. 

On May 30, 2025, the Supreme Court allowed the Trump administration to scrap the four-country scheme, which had permitted Fernandez and other Nicaraguans to secure permission to work in the US. 

Fernandez's contract with FIFA was terminated in October 2025, but she was paid a three-month salary as a bonus and remained illegally working as Infantino's housekeeper for the remainder of the year, according to the documents. 

In January 2026, Infantino allegedly asked Cordeiro, who was now working on the World Cup task force which operated directly out of Homeland Security, to leverage his new government contacts to secure Fernandez a new permit.

That same month, Fernandez was granted a new work visa and was re-hired as a FIFA employee on a $40,000-per-year contract until August.

FIFA and Cordeiro did not immediately respond to The Daily Mail's requests for comment. 

The Daily Mail also reached out to the DHS for comment and to question why Fernandez was granted a new work permit but did not receive an immediate response. 

The bombshell report comes after months of scrutiny for Infantino, who faces reelection in 2027. 

Infantino faced mutiny earlier this year over his secret plans – later scrapped – to sell a stake in the World Cup to private equity investors including Joshua Kushner, the brother of Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner.

It sparked uncertainty around Infantino's future after three confederations rejected his plan, which was then abandoned.

Among them was UEFA, which said it has lost confidence in Infantino and threatened to boycott future World Cups. 

Cordeiro also recently quit FIFA over Infantino's commercial deals with Josh Kushner's Thrive Capital. 

Infantino faced further scrutiny last month when it was alleged that Infantino personally intervened to suspend USA Folarin Balogun's World Cup red card following a call with President Trump.

In a saga that sparked condemnation from across the world, the striker was originally barred from the USA's last-16 match against Belgium, only for his ban to be sensationally suspended by the FIFA disciplinary committee following a protest by the White House. The New York Post claimed in October that Infantino told Trump in a call on July 1 that 'he would take care of it. One call and it was done.'

FIFA did not comment on the claims at the time but pointed to a July statement from Infantino, when he insisted the decision was made by ‘independent’ bodies acting ‘autonomously.’

Despite mounting pressure over recent months, Infantino intends to stand for a fourth consecutive term next March at the FIFA Congress.

news.title: Trump's Dismissed Epstein Letter Lawsuit Is the Latest Example of His Failure To State Cognizable Claims
news.text:
On July 17, 2025, The Wall Street Journal reported that a 2003 album marking the 50th birthday of financier Jeffrey Epstein, who would later be implicated in state and federal sex offenses involving underage girls, included a letter from Donald Trump, a longtime friend. The very next day, Trump sued the Journal in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida, saying "the supposed letter is a fake and the Defendants knew it when they chose to deliberately defame President Trump." The complaint sought compensatory and punitive damages "not less than $10 billion."

Last April, U.S. District Judge Darrin Gayles dismissed that lawsuit but let Trump try again with an amended complaint. On Saturday, Gayles dismissed the lawsuit again, this time with prejudice. In both cases, Gayles concluded that Trump's lawyers had fallen far short of alleging "actual malice," a crucial element of defamation cases involving public figures. That abject failure illustrates a persistent pattern in Trump's long history of frivolous lawsuits: As far as Trump is concerned, the point is to punish people for saying things he does not like, as opposed to seeking compensation for a legally cognizable injury.

What does "actual malice" mean? Trump seems to think it means that someone published a false statement "out of hatred and ill-will"—a phrase that appears in both Trump's original complaint against the Journal and in his amended complaint, which he filed on May 27, 2026. But as Gayles explains in his order, that is not what "actual malice" means.

"To plead actual malice," Gayles notes, quoting a 2018 decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 11th Circuit (which includes Florida), Trump "must allege facts sufficient to give rise to a reasonable inference that the false statement was made with knowledge that it was false or with reckless disregard of whether it was false or not. This is a subjective test, focusing on whether the defendant 'actually entertained serious doubts as to the veracity of the published account, or was highly aware that the account was probably false.'"

The Supreme Court established that standard in the 1964 case New York Times v. Sullivan, saying it was required by the First Amendment. "In these cases," the 11th Circuit noted in 2016, "there is a powerful interest in ensuring that free speech is not unduly burdened by the necessity of defending against expensive yet groundless litigation."

The actual malice standard "was designed to allow publishers the 'breathing
space' needed to ensure robust reporting on public figures and events," the 11th Circuit explained. "Forcing publishers to defend inappropriate suits through expensive discovery proceedings in all cases would constrict that breathing space in exactly the manner the actual malice standard was intended to prevent. The costs and efforts required to defend a lawsuit through that stage of litigation could chill free speech nearly as effectively as the absence of the actual malice standard altogether."

That explains why Gayles, after dismissing Trump's first complaint, rejected his motion for discovery "on issues related to actual malice." Specifically, Trump was keen to find evidence that might illuminate the defendants' "state of mind," which was sorely lacking in his original complaint. "President Trump's request to conduct discovery on issues related to actual malice before filing a well-pleaded complaint contravenes the purpose behind the actual malice standard," Gayles wrote.

Denied a license for that fishing expedition, Trump's lawyers tried again to file "a well-pleaded complaint," meaning their allegations, if true, would be sufficient to infer actual malice. But according to Gayles, they did not do any better this time around. "President Trump's conclusory allegations that Defendants acted with malice because they 'knew or should have known' the statements in the Article were false are insufficient to state a claim," he writes.

The amended complaint "appears to allege that by choosing to publish the Article despite President Trump's and his team's denials, Defendants acted with actual malice," Gayles says. "In effect, President Trump argues that once he declared the Letter a 'fake,' Defendants should have disregarded everything else they learned in their investigation and not published the story. But that is not what the actual malice standard requires and runs afoul of the First Amendment. Indeed, were that the law, any time a public figure or his team denies an accusation, journalists would be immediately blocked from publishing negative or contradictory press."

Trump argued that the Journal's investigation was inadequate. "A failure to investigate, without more, does not establish actual malice," Gayles notes. "Rather, 'a plaintiff must show the defendant deliberately avoided investigating the veracity of the statement in order to evade learning the truth.' The Amended Complaint comes nowhere close to this standard."

In fact, the Journal's article "details a thoughtful and detailed investigation," Gayles writes. "Before running the story, Defendants contacted President Trump and his team, Justice Department officials, and the FBI for comment. President Trump and his team responded with his denial [which was quoted in the article], the Justice Department did not respond at all, and the FBI declined to comment."

Journal reporters Khadeeja Safdar and Joseph Palazzolo tried to interview Ghislane Maxwell, the Epstein associate who solicited the messages for his birthday album, but she did not respond, and "her attorney stated that she was focused on her case before the Supreme Court" involving her federal sex trafficking conviction. In a July 2025 interview with the Justice Department, according to Trump's lawyers, Maxwell said "she did not remember President Trump submitting a letter for Epstein's 50th Birthday." Judging from that statement, Gayles says, "Maxwell had little to offer to Defendants' investigation."

Safdar and Palazzolo also "reached out to other individuals named in the Birthday
Book, including Leslie Wexner and Alan Dershowitz, and to individuals involved in binding the Birthday Book," Gayles notes. "In short, President Trump's allegation that Defendants failed to conduct an adequate investigation is rebutted by the Article
and is insufficient to establish actual malice."

The amended complaint "attempts to manufacture flaws" in the Journal's investigation, Gayles says, describing those efforts as "grasping at straws." The complaint, for example, faults Safdar and Palazzolo for "reviewing the Letter before publication" rather than "obtaining a copy of the Letter." But "nothing in the law suggests that Defendants needed to obtain, retain, or publish a copy."

Speaking of grasping at straws, the complaint charges Safdar and Palazzolo with "the intentional omission of the denial from President Trump regarding whether he signed the alleged letter or whether the signature on the alleged letter is authentic." Yet the article "states, multiple times, that President Trump denies writing the Letter and that '[i]t isn't clear how the letter with Trump's signature was prepared,'" Gayles notes. "This is more than sufficient to encompass any denial that he 'signed' the Letter or that the signature on the Letter is authentic."

In addition to Safdar, Palazzolo, and Dow Jones, which owns the Journal, Trump sued News Corporation, which owns Dow Jones; News Corporation CEO Robert Thomson; and Rupert Murdoch, the company's majority owner and emeritus chairman. But "other than stating that Dow Jones and News Corp published the Article 'at the direction of Defendants Murdoch and Thomson,'" Gayles notes, "the Amended Complaint is devoid of any allegations about how Thomson acted with actual malice."

Trump's disdain for meeting minimum legal requirements is part of a longstanding pattern. He has never been much concerned about actually winning in court, as opposed to inflicting pain on his enemies, whether he was demanding $500 million from an architecture critic who said unkind things about his plan for a Manhattan skyscraper, seeking $5 billion from a financial journalist who dared to question the extent of his wealth, suing a comedian for breach of contract based on a joke likening Trump to an orangutan, asserting that CNN defamed him by describing his reality-defying claims about the 2020 presidential election as "the Big Lie," alleging that The Des Moines Register committed consumer fraud by publishing poll results he did not like, or averring that CBS caused him $20 billion in damages by editing a 60 Minutes interview with Kamala Harris to make her seem slightly more cogent.

Although Trump plans to appeal Gayles' ruling, the Journal's editorial board said on Sunday, "the appeal isn't likely to succeed. A letter matching the Journal's description was released by Congressional investigators. Mr. Trump said he never wrote or signed the letter, but the Journal never claimed he did. It said only that the letter with the signature existed, and the Journal's stories have always included Mr. Trump's denials."

Trump "has long used lawsuits to intimidate the press, and most of the time he ends up losing," the editorial noted. "Mr. Trump, like other politicians, uses lawsuits to coerce settlements that he can tout as legal victories. He failed in this case because the Journal didn't roll over. A free press requires owners who back editors, and we couldn't do what we do without that support."
news.summary: The president's defamation case against The Wall Street Journal fits a pattern of frivolous litigation aimed at punishing speech that irks him.

news.title: 'If Donald Trump's Republicans do lose the midterms it will be entirely his fault'
news.text: Donald Trump's final public speech of the campaign was odd for a number of reasons. He stood on the banks of the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool on the eve of polls opening and talked, at length and in detail, about the refurbishment he's undertaken of the landmark. He reportedly cancelled tentative plans to close out the campaign with a rally in Grand Rapids, Michigan, as he has in all three of his presidential campaigns, in order to give this speech. And making most of your final message to voters about pool maintenance is unorthodox, to be sure. But there were other things. There were a few dozen people there - just invited guests and media. It looked small, especially given the association the backdrop has with the huge crowds for Martin Luther King's 'I have a dream' speech. Stay up to date with the latest breaking news in our US midterms 2026 live coverage . Trump delivered his remarks at the bottom of the steps that leading to the huge statue of Abraham Lincoln, forcing Trump to literally stand in the shadow of America's greatest president and look up at his stern face. It was unusually submissive, and maybe that's what caused a brief moment of self-reflection. "For some reason, the sitting president doesn't win the midterms," Trump said. "But we gave this a very strong shot." He's half right. The party controlling the White House almost always loses seats in the midterms - it's just a matter of how many. And how many is often linked to the President's approval rating. Since Trump properly joined the campaign, starting a 30-day trail of rallies that would exhaust a man half his age, Trump has begged his MAGA fanbase to pretend he's on the ballot, because in previous election turnout among 'low propensity' voters has been dramatically higher when he's a candidate. But this time, that hasn't helped. It may even have hurt. Trump's approval rating is historically bad. Some polls put it as low as 31%. The last President who went into a midterm election with approval numbers as bad as this was Truman in 1946, when his Democrats lost both houses to the Republicans, giving them control of congress for the first time in nearly two decades. There has been no discernible "Trump bump" in the polls for candidates who have been blessed with a rally in their district. And the rallies themselves have been torrid. Trump rallies are surprisingly camp affairs. The turnout is mostly pensioners, with a handful of chubby-faced young men. Everyone dresses up in novelty hats and tee shirts and waits in line for several hours, before being ushered in to listen to an elderly man tell jokes about men's posteriors. Then they dance to the YMCA and head home. If Trump had had the merest hint of message discipline in these rallies, it might have made a difference. But it was his indifference to the troubles of Americans, much of which was his doing, that sealed the deal. Trump has shown his age in this campaign. He's quicker to anger, gravelly in tone and he's cursing a lot more than he used to. And the tangents he famously weaves off into have become the show, not the sideshow. Instead of talking about the cost of living, he joked about cheeseburgers at his Florida resort costing $5,000. Instead of addressing the Iran war, and acknowledging his broken promise to stay out of international conflict, he bragged that America was making tonnes of money by siphoning oil out of Venezuela. And the 'America' he's talking about is billionaires and oil firms, not the regular joes and jills in his audience who are struggling at the pump. Instead of talking about issues that directly affect his base, he sank deep into the culture wars, invoking language so brazenly racist that Enoch Powell might have thought unwise to say in public. If the result is as bad for Trump as the polls predict, it will be almost entirely his fault. Not only has he failed to deliver on the promises he made during the campaign, he's actively, deliberately taken steps that have made things worse. And voters don't like that. It's tempting to say that like the Tories in 2024, this is an election that Trump lost, not one that Democrats won. But that doesn't tell the whole story. National voter enthusiasm for Democrats is low. But this campaign has seen some genuine future stars of the party rise to the surface. Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff looks like a Kennedy and has a way of combining soaring rhetoric and meticulous dissections of the Trump administration's corruption that I'm certain we'll see more of in the 2028 presidential campaign. In Michigan, Abdul El Sayed surprised many by being a raging lefty but also being fluent, confident and credible enough to overcome the racist attacks on his faith to connect with moderates. Not all of them, but enough. And if fresh-faced James Talarico managed to flip Texas, becoming the first Democrat senator the state has elected since 1988, the year before he was born, he'll have achieved what many people thought impossibel. Not least because the campaign of his opponent, Ken Paxton - who could not look and sound more like a vampire's familiar - was propped up with $168 million of Elon Musk's money. As polls opened, Trump was said to be optimistic about the results, hoping Republicans might just hold on to the House. But Trump does not like to lose. Historically, when he's had his back against the wall, the result has been ugly and violent. And with his temper shorter than ever, the coming days could prove a dangerous time for America.
news.summary: Trump has begged his MAGA fanbase to pretend he's on the ballot, because in previous election turnout among 'low propensity' voters has been dramatically higher when he's a candidate. But this time, that hasn't helped. It may even have hurt.

news.title: Ohio couple files $30M lawsuit saying they were injured when booted from a Trump midterm rally
news.text:
An Ohio couple has filed a federal civil rights lawsuit seeking $30 million in damages after alleging they were violently assaulted and ejected from one of President Donald Trump’s political rallies in Youngstown, according to new court documents.

The lawsuit, filed Wednesday in the U.S. District Court in Youngstown, names Ohio Lieutenant Governor Jon Husted, the City of Youngstown, event security company Ironwood LLC, Mahoning County Sheriff Jerry Greene and four unidentified sheriff’s deputies as defendants.

The plaintiffs, identified in the complaint as John and Jane Doe, allege that the defendants violated their constitutional protections against unreasonable search and seizure and infringed upon their First Amendment right to free speech, NBC affiliate WFMJ reported. The lawsuit further alleges counts of assault and battery.

The lawsuit stems from an October 12 event at the Covelli Centre, where the couple was attending a rally featuring the president. According to the complaint, the incident began when John Doe disrupted an address by Husted, vocalizing his opposition regarding congressional actions surrounding late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

John Doe shouted “Pedophile protector!” at the stage, claiming that congressional leaders were attempting to block the release of files related to the Epstein investigation, according to WFMJ. Jane Doe joined her husband in expressing dissent, though the complaint does not detail her specific statements.

Security personnel and law enforcement officers then moved to remove the couple from the venue. The complaint alleges that an officer approached John Doe from the side and “violently grabbed his head and neck and slammed him on the ground.” 

The physical confrontation resulted in John Doe’s glasses breaking and damage to his cell phone before he was “dragged” out of the facility, according to the filing.

Jane Doe claims in the filing that officers “assaulted and violently” removed her when she attempted to intervene to protect her husband. The complaint alleges that Husted continued his remarks from the podium without requesting that security personnel stop the removal.

The lawsuit states that security workers and law enforcement staff “berated and verbally attacked the Does” during the process. The couple also alleged a lack of immediate medical attention following the altercation.

A subsequent medical examination this week resulted in diagnoses for John Doe of a head injury and cervical sprain, with providers recommending follow-up treatment. The filing notes that John Doe is disabled, vision-impaired and asthmatic, and states that both plaintiffs “continue to suffer severe, traumatic injury, including, but not limited to, physical and mental harm and damage to family property.”

Following the rally, the couple filed initial incident reports with the East Canton Police Department, despite the event taking place within Youngstown municipal limits.

The lawsuit, assigned to U.S. District Court Judge Benita Pearson, requests preliminary and permanent injunctions, $5 million in compensatory damages, $25 million in punitive damages and reimbursement for legal costs.

In an emailed response to WFMJ regarding the litigation, Greene, the Mahoning County sheriff, defended the actions of his staff. 

“I am aware of the filing of this lawsuit,” Greene said. “I am extremely confident that my Deputies acted appropriately and followed the law. As this is now ongoing litigation, I am advised to not make any further comment.” 

The incident is the second ejection from the October 12 rally to draw scrutiny. Sheriff Greene previously initiated an internal review into a separate video recording that showed deputies removing another attendee, identified as Blake Miley. 

Miley was allegedly assaulted by a crowd member after revealing a shirt reading “Release the Epstein files.” Civil rights attorney Subodh Chandra announced he was representing Miley, though no formal lawsuit has been initiated.
news.summary: The plaintiffs claim they were forcibly tackled and dragged from the venue

news.title: Kalshi’s midterm trading tops $1.4 billion as traders bet on a Democratic sweep of Congress
news.text:
The site’s midterm forecasts are catnip for political junkies, but are also translating into big dollars: Kalshi’s midterm-related trading volume has surpassed $1.4 billion as of Tuesday, according to data supplied to Fortune. Leading the pack is a contract on whether Republicans or Democrats will control Congress, which has drawn $251 million in trading volume. A similar contract on which party will control the House has crossed the $181 million mark in trading volume. A separate market tracking all four possible combinations of House and Senate control has topped $112 million.

Closely watched races are also drawing action on these platforms, where traders can wager on everything from sports to politics. The Los Angeles mayoral race, which will decide whether Democrat Karen Bass gets a second term, has drawn just shy of $110 million in trading volume. Texas’ Senate race is also picking up steam, nearing the $100 million mark, with traders giving Democrat James Talarico a 71% chance of defeating Republican Ken Paxton. But the blue bets only go so far in Texas, where traders give incumbent Republican Greg Abbott a 65% chance of winning a gubernatorial contest that has drawn $21 million in trading volume. His challenger, Gina Hinojosa, is seeking to give Texas its first Democratic governor since 1995.

The surge in midterm trading builds on prediction markets’ breakout moment in 2024, when traders on popular platforms Kalshi and Polymarket favored Donald Trump as the winning candidate even as polls largely showed a toss-up. His victory helped turn the platforms into closely watched political barometers.

But their forecasting record has hit a few bumps, with recent misses raising questions about how much faith to put in the odds.

Last month, traders on Kalshi and Polymarket put their money on Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro, to unseat incumbent Lula da Silva. They gave Bolsonaro roughly an 80% chance of winning the presidential runoff—before the odds swung toward Lula as the results rolled in.

Wisconsin’s Democratic gubernatorial primary delivered another curveball in August, when traders gave Francesca Hong roughly a 95% chance of winning. Instead, David Crowley edged her out by less than half a percentage point. Polymarket later deleted a celebratory post touting Hong’s odds, while Kalshi’s founders defended the forecast with a reminder: “5% is not 0%.”
news.summary: From Texas to Los Angeles, traders are placing their bets. Recent surprises suggest the odds warrant caution.

news.title: BBC: Tre skenarët se si mund të përfundojnë zgjedhjet e mesmandatit në SHBA
news.text:
Pas muajsh fushate elektorale dhe miliarda dollarë të shpenzuar, amerikanët votojnë në zgjedhjet e mesmandatit, të cilat do të përcaktojnë përbërjen e Kongresit dhe raportin e forcave politike në dy vitet e fundit të mandatit të presidentit Donald Trump.

Sondazhet e fundit publike u japin përparësi demokratëve, por rezultatet e zgjedhjeve të mëparshme kanë treguar se parashikimet nuk janë gjithmonë të sakta. Sipas korrespondentit të BBC-së për Amerikën e Veriut, Anthony Zurcher, ekzistojnë tre skenarë kryesorë për mënyrën se si mund të përfundojë gara elektorale.

Një valë e madhe në favor të demokratëve

Skenari i parë parashikon një fitore të thellë të demokratëve, të cilët jo vetëm do të merrnin kontrollin e Dhomës së Përfaqësuesve, por do të tejkalonin ndjeshëm pragun prej 218 mandatesh të nevojshëm për shumicën.

Në këtë rast, demokratët mund të fitonin edhe në zona ku republikanët konsiderohen tradicionalisht të fortë, përtej garave që analistët i vlerësojnë si të pavendosura.

Faktorë që mund të ndikojnë në këtë rezultat janë pakënaqësia ndaj presidentit Trump, rritja e kostove për konsumatorët për shkak të luftës me Iranin, si dhe kundërshtitë ndaj disa politikave të administratës, përfshirë zbatimin agresiv të politikave të emigracionit dhe mbështetjen për ndërtimin e qendrave të të dhënave.

Një fitore e tillë mund t’u hapte demokratëve rrugën edhe drejt kontrollit të Senatit. Për këtë, ata do të duhej të fitonin shumicën e garave të pavendosura, përfshirë disa në shtete tradicionalisht konservatore.

Mes rezultateve që do të konsideroheshin veçanërisht të rëndësishme do të ishte fitorja në Teksas, ku demokratët nuk kanë fituar një garë për Senatin prej një brezi, ose në Kansas, ku një fitore e tillë nuk është regjistruar prej gati një shekulli.

Sipas këtij skenari, demokratët mund të siguronin një ose dy vende më shumë se shumica në Senat, duke shmangur edhe pasigurinë që mund të shkaktohej nga një sfidë ligjore e republikanëve në Alaskë.

Ky rezultat do të kërkonte pjesëmarrje të lartë të votuesve demokratë dhe mbështetje të konsiderueshme nga votuesit e pavarur. Gjithashtu, demokratët do të duhej të rikthenin një pjesë të mbështetjes së votuesve hispanikë dhe të rinjve, të cilët kishin votuar në favor të Trumpit në vitin 2024.

Një fitore e këtij përmasave do të përbënte një goditje të fortë politike për Trumpin dhe republikanët, duke krijuar terrenin për dy vite përplasjeje mes një Kongresi të kontrolluar nga demokratët dhe presidentit amerikan.

Shenjat e para që mund të tregojnë këtë skenar: Demokratët ruajnë avantazhin në garat e synuara në Florida dhe fitojnë disa zona republikane në Karolinën e Veriut, Miçigan, Nju Jork, Virxhinia dhe Kentaki. Një fitore në garën për Senatin në Karolinën e Jugut do të ishte një tjetër tregues i rëndësishëm.

Një fitore e kufizuar e demokratëve

Skenari i dytë parashikon që sondazhet të rezultojnë pjesërisht të sakta: demokratët marrin kontrollin e Dhomës së Përfaqësuesve, por me një shumicë të ngushtë.

Në këtë situatë, drejtuesit demokratë do të përballeshin me vështirësi për të siguruar votat e nevojshme për miratimin e ligjeve, pasi do të duhej të balanconin kërkesat e deputetëve të krahut të majtë me ato të përfaqësuesve më të moderuar të partisë.

Në Senat, demokratët mund të fitonin vetëm një ose dy vende shtesë, ndërsa garat në shtetet me prirje të fortë republikane do të rezultonin të paarritshme.

Sipas këtij parashikimi, ata mund të mos arrinin të mposhtnin senatoren republikane Susan Collins në Mein, ndërsa kandidati i krahut të majtë, Abdul El-Sayed, mund të mos arrinte të ruante vendin e Miçiganit në kampin demokrat.

Edhe polemika rreth dy kandidatëve me emrin Dan Sullivan në Alaskë mund të ndikonte në rezultatin e kandidates demokrate Mary Peltola.

Një element vendimtar në këtë skenar do të ishte pjesëmarrja e votuesve. Pjesëmarrja e lartë e demokratëve në votimin e hershëm do të duhej të shoqërohej me një mobilizim të fortë të republikanëve ditën e zgjedhjeve.

Përpjekjet e Trumpit për të nxitur bazën e tij elektorale në shtetet republikane mund ta ndihmonin partinë të shmangte një humbje të thellë. Si rezultat, Kongresi do të mbetej i ndarë mes dy forcave politike, duke rritur rrezikun e bllokimit të procesit legjislativ.

Shenjat e para që mund të tregojnë këtë skenar: Florida mbetet qartësisht në favor të republikanëve, ndërsa demokratët fitojnë disa vende në Dhomën e Përfaqësuesve në shtete si Virxhinia dhe Pensilvania. Në të njëjtën kohë, republikanët arrijnë të mbajnë mandatet në zonat ku kanë një avantazh më të konsoliduar.

Një natë e mirë për republikanët

Skenari i tretë parashikon që republikanët të ruajnë kontrollin e të dyja dhomave të Kongresit, pavarësisht avantazhit që sondazhet u japin demokratëve.

Për të ndodhur kjo, sondazhet do të duhej të kishin nënvlerësuar sërish mbështetjen për Trumpin, ndërsa garat e pavendosura do të duhej të përfundonin kryesisht në favor të republikanëve.

Kjo do të kërkonte një pjesëmarrje më të lartë se sa pritej të votuesve republikanë, si dhe rikthimin në kampin e Trumpit të një pjese të votuesve të pavarur dhe hispanikë, të cilët në sondazhet e fundit kanë shfaqur pakënaqësi ndaj politikave të tij.

Në këtë skenar, gara për Dhomën e Përfaqësuesve mund të mbetet e hapur deri në numërimin e votave me postë në Kaliforni, proces që mund të zgjasë disa ditë.

Republikanët mund të siguronin në fund një shumicë të ngushtë, të ndihmuar edhe nga ndryshimet në hartat e zonave zgjedhore në shtete si Teksasi, Florida dhe Karolina e Veriut, të cilat synojnë t’u japin atyre avantazh elektoral.

Në Senat, republikanët mund të fitonin të gjitha garat në shtetet konservatore dhe të merrnin gjithashtu Miçiganin, një vend që deri në zgjedhje mbahej nga demokratët.

Edhe nëse nuk arrijnë të fitojnë në Karolinën e Veriut apo në shtete si Minesota dhe Nju Hempshër, ku demokratët kanë kontrollin politik, republikanët mund t’i mbajnë garat konkurruese deri në fund.

Nëse ky skenar realizohet, Trump mund ta interpretojë rezultatin si një mandat të ri elektoral për politikat e tij të brendshme dhe të jashtme, duke vijuar agjendën e administratës me mbështetjen e një Kongresi të kontrolluar nga republikanët.
