news.title: After ICE Terror, Poll Finds 61 Percent of Latino Voters Say They’ll Vote Blue
news.text:
In 2024, Donald Trump won the presidency with the support of 44% of Hispanic voters, suggesting that a major realignment in party preferences might be underway. But just two years later, it appears much of that support has eroded. Sixty-one percent of Hispanic voters say they will now support Democrats in the midterms, including 11% who previously had voted for President Trump.

We get a bird’s-eye view of what to expect from the Latino vote from Marisa Franco, the co-founder and director of the advocacy organization Mijente. While ICE brutality will be at the front of voters’ minds, she says, Democrats cannot continue to take Latino voters for granted. “The vast majority of Latinos are working-class. Quite simply, they voted for Trump because they were looking at issues of economy, cost, inflation,” explains Franco. “And at the end of the day, these same issues have worsened under Trump’s administration, under Republican control. So people, I think, are looking for someone who’s going to explain what’s happening and propose solutions and be dogged about finding them.”

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org.

We end today’s show looking at how Latino voters could impact today’s midterms. In 2024, President Trump won the presidency with the support of 44% of Latino voters across the country — a significant shift following decades of Democratic advantage among Latinos. Two years later, it appears much of those Republican gains have eroded, and Democratic voters are significantly more motivated to go to the polls. Polling suggests cost of living is the top concern for all voters, including Latinos, who now trust Democrats more than President Trump to manage the economy. But the Trump administration’s violent crackdown on immigrants has also hurt his support among Latinos.

This is a former Trump supporter in Miami, Wayne DeMario, whose wife Yamile, who is Cuban, was recently deported to Mexico.

WAYNE DEMARIO: I am praying that everybody votes these pieces of garbage out. That’s it. Team up, everybody. I don’t care. Don’t be afraid that you voted for this jerk. Don’t be afraid that you voted for this guy. Team up and vote against him. Don’t worry about losing your guns. You’re not going to lose your guns if you vote Democrat. You’re not going to lose anything. Matter of fact, if I would have voted Democrat, I wouldn’t have lost my wife.

AMY GOODMAN: To talk about this and more, we’re joined by Marisa Franco, co-founder and director of Mijente, a national digital organizing hub for Latinx and Chicanx communities, joining us from Houston, Texas.

Thanks so much, Marisa, for being there. The New York Times has said Latinos are the most important swing vote in today’s election, making up 20% of registered voters in two dozen highly competitive House races, from Arizona, California, Colorado, Florida, Pennsylvania, Texas and other states. Can you talk about the shift that we’re seeing from 2024?

MARISA FRANCO: It’s good to be with you, Amy.

Yeah, it’s going to be a big night. The forecasts show a 15-point swing towards Democrats from Latinos and in heavy Latino districts. Just a quick roll call. You look at Florida, a place that oftentimes people have counted out as gone to the right. I’m really looking at the Boricua vote in Florida. I’m looking at Venezolanos, who were heavily hit by ICE. You just heard the gentleman talking about the impact of ICE and deportations on himself personally, feeling that, that Trump remorse, that MAGA remorse.

Georgia and North Carolina, and just overall in the Southeast, I’m looking at Latinos continuing to advance. I think you’re going to be looking — I’m really paying attention of, like, where are we making advancements and where are we helping break through. Georgia and North Carolina, I think you’ve seen the growth of Latino populations and actually be a flank and, what I would affectionately say, being helpers and not hurters, not only in Georgia and North Carolina, but also in Mississippi in a key race there.

Then we go to the Sun Belt — New Mexico, Colorado, Nevada and my home state of Arizona — where I am hoping that voters in southern Arizona take out “el trumpitas” Juan Ciscomani out of the House.

And then, last but not least, Texas, which I think could be the story of the night for the Latino vote. We have Democratic candidates who are knocking on the door. No Democratic candidate has won statewide in Texas for over 30 years. The early vote nationally is up 44% in comparison to the ’22 midterms. A big chunk of that is young voters, infrequent voters. That is the case here in Texas.

So, the question tonight is going to be: Will these numbers get at presidential levels, or will we surpass the early vote from ’22? Which candidates will voters go for? And what is the message they’re sending to the Trump administration?

AMY GOODMAN: So, talk about, from the deadly immigration raids to the spiraling economy due to Trump’s war on Iran, how those who supported Trump in 2024 shifted their views. And what does it take for Democrats to keep that support, Marisa?

MARISA FRANCO: So, I think it’s important to understand that Latinos, overall, are very, very working-class. The vast majority of Latinos are working-class. Quite simply, they voted for Trump because they were looking at issues of economy, cost, inflation. The people talk about the price of eggs. And, you know, we can talk about Trump’s overreach, but, in essence, what voters are looking at is impact. And at the end of the day, these same issues have worsened under Trump’s administration, under Republican control.

So people, I think, are looking for someone who’s going to explain what’s happening and propose solutions and be dogged about finding them. I think that it is an assumption to believe that whatever happens in this election, that Latinos are back in the Democratic tent for good. I believe that over the last election cycles, Latinos have been showing — declaring, in essence, their independence from partisan politics. And so, I think that the issues that they’re really caring about in this election is the cost of living, the war, opposition to the war, and ICE and what they’ve been doing in communities across this country.

AMY GOODMAN: Now, what are you doing about the possibility of voter suppression? ICE is supposedly not going to be deployed to the polls. We don’t know what’s actually going to happen. But other federal agents, about a thousand, are being sent to the polls across the country. What is Mijente and other Latinx groups doing?

MARISA FRANCO: You know, in some ways, I look at the Trump administration, I follow the moniker in Spanish, ”Más vale pedir perdón que pedir permiso. And that is, it’s easier to ask for forgiveness than permission. I think sometimes they don’t even ask for forgiveness. So, they’re saying they’re not going to be there. Who knows? I think there is a robust operation across the country of election protection. This has been an issue over several cycles. People will be on alert.

In our community, the damage has been done. It’s not only election, but they have been terrorizing our communities. There was incidents in the Central Valley, where you have a race, David Valadao, Republican, versus Randy Villegas, where ICE was in the community, was door knocking, supposedly looking at election fraud. Those are reports we got from the ground weeks ago. People are on alert.

And all we can do is urge people to come out and to have — you know, to utilize the infrastructure and the operations that have been set forth. But we cannot allow them to intimidate us from exercising our democratic right to vote, and ideally to vote them out.

AMY GOODMAN: Marisa Franco, co-founder and director of Mijente, a national digital organizing hub for Latinx and Chicano communities.

Tune in tonight for Democracy Now!’s four-hour live election night special, starting at 8 p.m. Eastern. We’ll be streaming live at democracynow.org, also on our YouTube channel. Check your local Democracy Now! station for listings.

Oh, and Steal This Story, Please!, the documentary about Democracy Now!, is available now in the United States and Canada on many streaming platforms, from Amazon Prime to YouTube to Apple TV. Go to StealThisStory.org, and you can see where you can watch it. And check our website for where it is in theaters still.

Democracy Now! produced with Mike Burke, Deena Guzder, Anjali Kamat, Messiah Rhodes, Nicole Salazar, Nermeen Shaikh, María Taracena, John Hamilton, Sara Nasser, Charina Nadura, Sam Alcoff, Tey-Marie Astudillo, Robby Karran, Hany Massoud, Laura Bustillos and Diego Ramos. Our executive director is Julie Crosby. I’m Amy Goodman.
news.summary: However, warns the director of the advocacy organization Mijente, Democrats can’t take Latino voters for granted.
news.author: Amy Goodman

news.title: US voters head to polls to deliver midterm verdict on Trump
news.text:
DETROIT: Americans headed to the polls in Tuesday’s midterm elections to deliver a verdict on the first two years of President Donald Trump’s second term, with surveys and nonpartisan analysts favoring Democrats to wrest the House of Representatives from Republicans while control of the Senate remains uncertain.

The battle for the Senate is unfolding across nearly 10 closely contested statewide races, most in Republican strongholds.

History is against Trump’s Republicans: the sitting president’s party has lost ground in Congress in all but two midterm elections since World War Two. Trump’s approval rating is hovering near his all-time lows, dragged down by deep voter frustration over the war with Iran and the resulting rise in fuel prices.

There is little doubt this year’s election is all about Trump, who is nearly two years into his second term. Trump himself has told his supporters repeatedly to “pretend I’m on the ballot,” a message Democratic leaders have happily echoed.

Trump touted in a television interview on Tuesday morning what he billed as his achievements in Venezuela and Iran and declared optimism for fellow Republicans.

In remarks that appeared aimed at swaying voters unhappy with US support for Israel, Trump said that he intended to stop $3.8 billion in promised annual funding to Israel after the end of this year, but it was unclear how he would do so, given a 2020 law mandating the funding levels in the agreement with Israel.

US policy toward Israel has been a particular focus in Michigan, where progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed is running a closely watched campaign for Senate.

The president has sought to energize his base with more than two dozen campaign rallies since the start of October, most in states he easily won in 2024.

Led by Trump, Republicans have portrayed Democratic candidates as radical, un-American and even communist.

But opinion polls show voters are most concerned about affordability, and disapprove of Trump’s handling of the issue after his sweeping tariffs on imports, many of which were thrown out as illegal by the courts, and his decision to attack Iran in February increased domestic costs.

Republican candidates, meanwhile, have struggled to distance themselves from a president who demands fealty and rarely acknowledges mistakes.

At a voting center in a predominantly Black neighborhood in northwest Detroit, Natalia Towns, 34, said she did not find efforts by Mike Rogers, the Republican Senate candidate, to court Black voters sincere, and felt El-Sayed would do more to bring down costs.

“I do feel like health matters, gas prices are high, food is too high,” she said.

Doj deploys election monitors

Democrats have warned that Trump, who has long falsely claimed that US elections are rigged, may attempt to challenge Tuesday’s results if Republicans lose.

The US Justice Department said on Tuesday it was deploying 1,000 election monitors and observers to all 50 states in what it called the largest Election Day monitoring effort in history.

Democrats have criticized the plan as potential voter intimidation. Roughly two-thirds of the jurisdictions the department listed are in places where voters supported Democrat Kamala Harris over Trump in the 2024 presidential election, a Reuters analysis found.

All 435 seats in the US House of Representatives are up for election, along with 35 of the Senate’s 100 seats, though most contests are not considered competitive. Democrats must flip at least three House seats and four Senate seats to win a majority in each chamber.

Democrats have little margin for error. The party must defend all of its current seats while winning at least two states that voted for Trump by a double-digit margin two years ago: Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, Ohio, South Carolina and Texas.

Opinion polls show Democrats either narrowly leading or within striking distance in all of those states.

Election drama in michigan, alaska, texas

The Michigan Senate contest between El-Sayed, 42, and Rogers, 63, represents a high-profile test of whether Republicans’ identity-based attacks û El-Sayed would be the nation’s first Muslim senator ù prove effective in a battleground state.

A win for El-Sayed, who has criticized Israel and supports policies such as universal healthcare, would also be seen as a boost for the Democratic Party’s left wing ahead of the 2028 presidential election.

The Alaska Senate race has been thrown into turmoil after the New York Times reported that the campaign of Democratic candidate Mary Peltola, 53, helped recruit a third candidate who shares the first and last name of her Republican opponent, Dan Sullivan, 61.

Peltola has denied involvement. Trump’s Justice Department has launched a criminal probe into the allegations and filed a lawsuit to block certification of the election results, though a judge dismissed the latter effort.

In addition to its actions in Alaska, Trump’s Justice Department also filed a lawsuit in California to block ballots it says may be invalid, a break from decades of practice meant to insulate elections from political interference. The US Supreme Court on Monday rejected the administration’s request for an emergency order in the case.

In Texas, Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico, 37, has his party once again dreaming of winning the biggest Republican state after decades of heartbreak. His scandal-plagued opponent, Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton, 63, has benefited from a nine-figure investment from the world’s richest man, Elon Musk, who has spent hundreds of millions of dollars boosting Republicans.

In Kansas, Democrat Adam Hamilton, 62, a megachurch pastor, holds a narrow polling lead over Republican US Senator Roger Marshall, 66. The state voted for Trump by more than 16 percentage points in 2024 and has not elected a Democratic senator in nearly a century.

And in Maine, Republican US Senator Susan Collins, 73, is once again seeking to defy the Democratic leanings of her home state and win a sixth term. She faces Democrat Troy Jackson, 58, a former state senate president who unexpectedly became the nominee after Democratic oyster farmer Graham Platner dropped out amid accusations of misconduct, which he denied.

There are 47 US House races widely seen as competitive, according to a Reuters analysis of the leading election forecasters. If the other contests all proceed as predicted, Democrats would need to win only 13 of those races to secure a majority.

The fight for the House has been waged largely on Republican turf, including some districts Trump carried by double digits in 2024. A Trump-backed Republican effort to redraw districts in several states to make them safer for the party appears not to have yielded the gains the president expected.

news.title: From Haley Stevens to AOC: How 2020’s Rising Stars Have Fared
news.text: Like many people in political circles, Charlotte Alter watched in disbelief on Sunday as Democratic Representative Haley Stevens announced that she was endorsing Mike Rogers, the Republican nominee in the race for a U.S. Senate seat in Michigan. “For as long as I’ve known her she’s prided herself on being a loyal Dem team player, and now she’s torching that entire career and reputation in a single day,” Alter, a journalist and author, wrote on X. “Absolutely wild to watch a political career implode in such a destructive way.” Alter’s view on Stevens’ November surprise—a decision called “despicable” by Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York and brave by President Donald Trump—is worth paying attention to. She wrote The Ones We’ve Been Waiting For, a 2020 book that profiled 10 millennial rising stars in politics as a way of examining a generation beginning to take power in an America dominated by a gerontocracy apparently unmoored from reality and the needs of the people. Newsweek contacted Alter for comment. In the introduction to her book, Alter made clear she was not attempting to predict the future careers of her subjects but using them to offer a preview of what America could look like with millennials in charge. Stevens was one subject of the book, alongside widely recognized names such as Pete Buttigieg, who was transportation secretary under President Joe Biden, and Republican Representative Elise Stefanik of New York, and less well-known local figures who seemed poised for bigger things. Six years later, their fortunes have diverged dramatically. Some rose to national prominence, while others left elected politics and several saw seemingly unstoppable careers suddenly derailed. Careers Crashing Back to Earth Stevens provides the most spectacular example. The former Obama administration official was part of Democrats’ celebrated 2018 House class and won reelection three times before giving up her seat to run for Senate this year. After narrowly losing the Democratic primary to Abdul El-Sayed, she pledged to support him, only to endorse Rogers two days before Tuesday's general election following an increasingly bitter dispute over Israel and El-Sayed’s political allies. Two of the book’s Republican subjects have also discovered how quickly political fortunes can change. Former Navy SEAL Dan Crenshaw arrived in Congress in 2019, seemingly tailor-made for national Republican politics. Instead, he lost his primary in March to Texas state Representative Steve Toth, becoming the first congressional incumbent denied renomination this cycle. Crenshaw had supported Ukraine aid and rejected claims that the 2020 election was stolen, while President Donald Trump declined to endorse him. While Crenshaw zigged, Stefanik zagged, transforming from a comparatively moderate Republican into one of Trump’s fiercest congressional allies. She replaced Liz Cheney in House GOP leadership and was nominated by Trump to become U.N. ambassador before he withdrew the nomination, citing Republicans’ narrow House majority. And more setbacks were to come. She launched a bid for New York governor last November, abandoned it weeks later and announced she would not seek another House term. The Ones Who Rose When the book appeared, Buttigieg was concluding his improbable campaign for the Democratic presidential nomination. He subsequently served four years as President Joe Biden’s transportation secretary and is again one of the party’s most prominent national figures. This year, Buttigieg has campaigned across the country for Democrats while leaving open a possible White House bid in 2028. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, meanwhile, has evolved from insurgent newcomer into one of the most recognizable Democrats in America. The New York representative won her 2026 primary with nearly 87 percent of the vote and remains firmly entrenched in her heavily Democratic district. Ocasio-Cortez’s ascendancy has also brought speculation about a potential presidential run in 2028, which could put her in the same Democratic primary field as Buttigieg. Lauren Underwood’s rise has been less flashy but perhaps equally telling. The Illinois congresswoman, who became the youngest Black woman to serve in Congress when she took office in 2019 at age 32, is now a member of the House Appropriations Committee and co-chair of the House Democratic Policy and Communications Committee. Finding Power Elsewhere Eric Lesser was a Massachusetts state senator and former Obama White House aide when Alter profiled him. He ran for lieutenant governor in 2022, lost the Democratic primary and left the state Legislature. He now works as senior counsel at law firm WilmerHale. Max Rose didn’t stay long in Congress. The Army veteran flipped a Staten Island-based seat in New York for Democrats in 2018, lost it to Republican Nicole Malliotakis in 2020 and lost a rematch two years later. He remains in politics, however, serving as a senior adviser to VoteVets and, in a distinctly 2026 turn, advising Leading the Future, a political group backed by AI industry figures. Braxton Winston was a Charlotte city councilman in North Carolina when Alter wrote about him. He later became mayor pro tem and was the Democratic nominee for North Carolina labor commissioner in 2024, losing with 47.25 percent of the vote. Last year, he was elected president of the North Carolina State AFL-CIO. Svante Myrick became mayor of Ithaca, New York, at just 24. He left City Hall in 2022 and now leads the progressive organization People for the American Way. Winston and Myrick followed neither the traditional ladder from local government to Congress nor statewide office. Both instead found political influence outside elected government. A Generation Scattered Six years is a long time in politics. The period since Alter’s book was published has encompassed the COVID-19 pandemic, two presidential elections, the January 6, 2021, riot at the U.S. Capitol, the end of the Biden presidency, Trump’s return to the White House and profound changes in both major parties. Those upheavals altered not only the country Alter was writing about, but the political paths available to the generation she profiled. Some climbed the traditional ladder. Others discovered it had been pulled away, chose to step off it or found different ways to wield influence. And then there is Stevens, whose extraordinary break with her own party on the eve of the 2026 midterms prompted Alter to liken it to the Invasion of the Body Snatchers, a film in which alien duplicates replace the residents of a small California town. Taken together, the 10 no longer look much like a single political generation moving together toward power. They look instead like a snapshot of a generation scattered in different directions by six tumultuous years in American politics. For more analysis from Daniel on the numbers shaping U.S. politics and the 2026 midterms, sign up for Newsweek's Midterms Monitor newsletter. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Daniel Orton and Dave Siminoff.
news.summary: Haley Stevens' stunning GOP endorsement offers a window into what happened to 10 rising political stars profiled six years ago.

news.title: What Voters Care About As US Midterms Go Underway
news.text: AFP has deployed reporters, photographers and video journalists across the United States as American voters head to the polls for crucial midterm elections.Here is a round-up of interviews on Tuesday at polling stations where voters agreed to share their thoughts about what was on their minds and motivating their choices.Hopeful DemocratsWith polling data suggesting the Democratic Party is on track to capture a majority in the House of Representatives and perhaps even in the Senate, many left-leaning voters said they were hopeful about the results."Two years ago was a really devastating outcome for me," Emma Mondadori, a 39-year-old who works in philanthropy, told AFP in Brooklyn, New York, referring to President Donald Trump's election."I've been really looking forward to this day where we get to have a say again in the future of our country... I'm cautiously hopeful, optimistic."The Cost Of LivingWith gasoline prices up by a third since last year and diesel nearly double -- not to mention sharp food price inflation -- everyday spending was on many people's minds."It's about the cost of living, gas prices, those kind of things. It needs to change for the everyday person, and I'm an everyday person," Donta Comer, a 38-year-old project manager in Atlanta, Georgia, told AFP.Tom, a 27-year-old businessman at the same polling station who declined to give his surname, agreed."Everyone, at least in my generation, is a little frustrated with the affordability crisis and gas prices and what's going on abroad," added the non-partisan voter.Leadership ReferendumMid-term elections are typically seen as a form of referendum on the sitting president.And few leaders have polarized public opinion as strongly as Donald Trump."I'm independent but I voted Democrat, I just wanted to go back into the culture of decency, integrity, honesty, and the rest follows," Yan Cardineau, 59, told AFP in Austin, Texas. "If we lose that, it doesn't matter how much money you make."Estrella Roque, a 69-year-old voter of Cuban origin, told AFP in Miami she had voted Republican."What I like about the Republicans is that they can fix the country," she explained in Spanish. "Donald Trump hasn't been given time to show who he really is."ImmigrationIn his final pitch to voters, Trump has stressed his success in reducing immigration and stopping crossings along the southern border with Mexico.While his tough stance plays well with his core supporters, others have been put off by the brutal tactics used by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents."I am very concerned about climate change, school violence and the situation with people who still don't have immigration status in this country," Diana Alvarez, a 38-year-old Cuban-born attorney said in Doral, Florida."It's tough for any presidency, but this one in particular has been a little violent and aggressive (with migrants) and I don't think that was necessary."IranTrump's most consequential foreign policy decision of his second term -- the February 28 attack on Iran along with Israel -- was referenced by several voters."It's discouraging. Again, promises made, promises not kept. 'No new wars' was the mantra," Wes Pyron, a 37-year-old who works at an environmental health nonprofit in Washington, said."I don't understand what we're doing there, objectives aren't clear, priorities aren't clear."Fears Of SocialismMany Republican candidates and Trump have sought to portray their Democratic rivals as dangerous tax-and-spend Socialists intent on destroying American capitalism."A lot of today's younger people think socialism is the way to go," Daryl Ruley, an 84-year-old in Austin, Texas, told AFP. "They don't understand history if they believe that's the case."Maru Restrepo, a 70-year-old voter of Colombian origin in Miami, said Democrats had become "very Socialist, Communist, and Muslim."MichiganIn one of the most widely watched races for the Senate -- in Michigan -- Democrat candidate Abdul El-Sayed has made free universal healthcare and ending US support for Israel key planks of his platform.The Muslim former medical administrator has been called a jihadist by Trump and has been smeared with accusations of sympathizing with Islamist groups such as the Muslim Brotherhood or Hamas."We just got to get it done because we all need help. I need help," said Makeyla Borndes, a 51-year-old former teacher who was forced to retire after falling down a staircase.She wore several El-Sayed pins on her green apron and neon pink socks.(Except for the headline, this story has not been edited by NDTV staff and is published from a syndicated feed.)

news.title: America votes in midterm elections
news.text: Americans began voting on Tuesday in one of the most consequential elections in recent times, widely seen as a referendum on Donald Trump’s presidency that has been marked by a prolonged war in Iran, rising inflation, trade wars and deep divisions in society.On polling day, Trump sprung a surprise by announcing that the US will stop providing Israel USD four billion in aid from next year, which Democrat Ro Khanna described as a desperate attempt to stave off a “Blue tsunami”.The polling will decide whether President Trump’s Republican Party retains control of the House of Representatives and the Senate, the two chambers of the US Congress, or, as opinion polls are predicting, the Democratic Party wrests control of at least the House if not the Senate, also in the final two years of Trump’s second term in office.Polling began Tuesday at 6:00 am. Eastern time in Indiana and Kentucky, and staggered across time zones in the US. Polling began in California at 7:00 am local time (10:00 am Eastern) and in Alaska at 11:00 Eastern Time.On the eve of the elections, the US launched limited strikes on Iran’s Qesham Island in the Hormuz Strait. Officials said that the strikes were in response to Iran firing at a US aircraft.At stake in the elections are all 435 seats of the House and 37 seats in the 100-member Senate.Elections are also being held for the post of Governor in 36 states, including in Ohio, where Indian American Vivek Ramaswamy is locked in a keen contest with his rival and Democratic nominee Amy Acton.The first results are expected to trickle in from 5:00 am on Wednesday (India Time).A number of Indian American candidates are in the electoral fray for posts ranging from Governor to city council members. Democrat Nithya Raman, who was born in Kerala, is locked in a keen contest with her former boss Karen Bass for the post of Mayor of Los Angeles, the second-largest city in the US.Indian-American lawmakers Ro Khanna, Ami Bera, Pramila Jayapal and Suhas Subramanyam are seeking re-election to the US House of Representatives, while fellow Democrats Pia Dandiya and Amish Shah are in the fray in competitive races to make their debut as Congresspersons.On Monday, the Republicans and the Democrats made their final pitch to the voters, with Trump choosing an unusual venue - the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool - to focus on the renovations undertaken in the national capital instead of talking about tax cuts, tariffs and border security, which have been the high points of his election rallies.According to the White House, Trump did a whirlwind tour of 20 states, mostly Republican strongholds, to address 30 rallies in the last 32 days. Analysts say his approval ratings are at an all-time low, and he has become a liability to Republican candidates.If the pre-poll forecasts come true and Democrats take control of the US Congress, it will allow for deeper Congressional scrutiny and checks of Trump’s actions, which will severely limit his ability to push his agenda. He will, however, retain the power to govern through executive orders, which will be valid for two years.“We are reaching a boiling point in the country as a whole. There are the elites, the ruling class, the Epstein class that is truly 1 per cent that is wealthy, and there is the rest of us,” Shuchita Patel, a Democrat, who is running for the post of Forsyth County Commissioner, told PTI.Trump acknowledged the possibility of his wings being clipped but indicated that he will not allow Congress to slow him down.“I guess I’ll become Mr Veto,” Trump told the New York Post’s Pod Force One podcast in response to a question on Republicans losing control of both Houses of the US Congress, referring to the presidential power to veto actions by Congress.Former President Barack Obama boosted the Democratic campaign with rallies in Ohio, Michigan and Georgia, which clearly left Trump rattled.“This election is our last, best chance of at least reining him in, reining in some of the foolishness of this administration,” Obama said in Georgia last week.“It’s the circuit-breaker in the system, and we need to flip it,” he said, taking Trump to task for focusing on White House renovations instead of issues affecting the people.The upbeat Democrats, however, suffered an unexpected setback in the eleventh hour when Congresswoman Haley Stevens of Michigan crossed over to the Republican side on Sunday, breaking ranks with Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, who could be the first Muslim elected to the US Senate.The Democratic Party quickly rallied behind El-Sayed, issuing statements condemning Stevens, who surprised many by endorsing El-Sayed’s Republican rival, Mike Rogers, and appearing alongside him in public.Stevens lost in the Senate primary to El-Sayed. She is a staunch supporter of Israel, while El-Sayed is a fierce critic of the US ally.The Democrats are hoping to flip seven Senate seats -- Michigan, Maine, Ohio, Kansas, Texas, Iowa and Alaska -- in their bid to gain a majority in the 100-member House.Each of the 50 states in the United States is represented by two Senators who sit in the Congress for a six-year term. But the Senators are divided into three lots, and their terms are staggered so that elections are held every two years.The House members are elected for a two-year term.Republicans enjoy a majority in both chambers of Congress, but by thin margins.In the House of Representatives, Speaker Mike Johnson has 218 Republicans and one independent, Kevin Kiley of California, against 214 Democrats, with two seats vacant.The Senate is split 53-47 in favour of the Republicans. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to wrest control of the chamber. Of the 35 Senate seats on the ballot, 22 are held by Republicans.The mid-term elections are also crucial for Vice President J D Vance, who is burnishing his credentials to become a successor to Trump’s mantle.Vance made campaign stops in New York and Ohio on Monday, where Republicans were fighting for House and Senate seats.He highlighted Trump’s moves to end taxes on tips and overtime and secure the border while branding Democrats as “lunatics” who have contempt for American voters.About 210 million Americans are registered to vote, according to USAF acts. California has the most registered voters, with 23.2 million, followed by Texas (17.4 million) and Florida (13.6 million). Together, they account for about 26 per cent of all registered voters.Wyoming (278,468), Vermont (459,455) and Alaska (603,310) have the fewest.According to the AP, more than 57 million ballots have been cast in 47 states and D.C. as of Monday, compared to a little under 44.5 million in 49 states and D.C. in 2022.

news.title: Here’s how past midterm flips in Congress have impacted taxpayers
news.text:
With polls predicting at least the Senate or House will flip for Democrats in the midterm elections, many voters are looking to Congress for big change in the coming years. 

Democratic House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has vowed that his party will aim to end the Iran war, undo the Trump administration’s Medicaid cuts, and repeal the president’s tariffs. 

“The entirety of the House Democratic caucus understands what the stakes are in terms of defeating MAGA extremism in November and then, as Democrats, getting off to a fast start in January,” Jeffries said in September. 

Over the past 32 years, flipping the House or Senate for either party has led to major tax changes, including the birth of key tax credits and deductions that are still active today. 

While some experts have warned of legislative standoffs in the coming years, history shows bipartisan change for taxpayers is possible. 

Some 32 years ago, Republicans took control of the House and Senate for the first time in four decades, leading to extensive budget and tax discussions between Republican leadership and Democratic President Bill Clinton. 

Bipartisan action led to the Taxpayer Relief Act of 1997, landmark legislation that created the Roth IRA, Child Tax Credit, lifetime learning credit, and reduced the top tax rate for capital gains from 28 percent to 20 percent. 

At the time, nonpartisan think tank The Tax Foundation estimated that the act would save taxpayers $95.3 billion in tax payments in the five years after the legislation went into effect. 

“It is a fair plan that places a priority on education tax cuts and provides a child tax credit to families who work hard and pay taxes,” Clinton said when he signed the act on August 5, 1997. “It also incorporates Republican priorities in a good-faith effort to honor the budget accord and to reach final agreement on a tax cut the American people deserve.”

Democrats took control of the House and Senate for the first time since the 1992 midterm elections. One year later, Republican President George W. Bush signed the Fair Minimum Wage Act of 2007 on May 25. 

The legislation boosted the federal minimum wage from $5.15 to $7.25 an hour over two years. It went from $5.15 to $5.85 after 60 days of the legislation being enacted; from $5.85 to $6.55 12 months after the first increase; and from $6.55 to $7.25 two years later. 

The act also included tax incentives for small businesses, an essential part of Bush's support for the minimum wage increase pushed by Democrats. 

“The Administration appreciates the Senate Finance Committee's willingness to respond in a bipartisan fashion to the President's call to enact a minimum wage increase matched with tax relief for small businesses,” the Bush administration said in early 2007. 

Republicans gained control of the House halfway through President Barack Obama’s first term, and this set off a battle between the House and Senate over budgets that nonpartisan think tank Brookings Institute called “fiscal fights.” 

Those clashes resulted in the bipartisan Tax Relief, Unemployment Insurance Reauthorization and Job Creation Act of 2010, which extended George W. Bush-era tax cuts, recession-related unemployment benefits, and several other tax-related provisions for another two years. 

During Obama’s second term, Congress passed the 2012 American Taxpayer Relief Act, which made many of Bush’s temporary tax cuts for lower- and moderate-income taxpayers permanent, according to the nonpartisan Center on Budget and Policy Priorities. 

The midterms during President Donald Trump’s first term led to Democrats winning the House, blocking Republicans’ agenda for the back half.

“It effectively prevented Republicans from advancing several items in their agenda, such as another major round of tax cuts,” Sherman Standberry, a certified public accountant and CEO of tax firm My CPA Coach, told The Independent in an email. 

Democrats protected individual tax cuts in Trump's 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act and played a key role in passing the bipartisan Setting Every Community Up for Retirement Enhancement (SECURE) Act of 2019. 

The act made saving for retirement more accessible, financial firm Fidelity pointed out in an analysis of the SECURE Act.

With additional reporting from The Associated Press
news.summary: While some experts are warning of legislative standoffs in the coming years, history shows bipartisan change for taxpayers is possible

news.title: Report: Israel warns US that Iran may use chemical weapons against regional adversaries
news.text: Israel has warned the United States that intelligence indicates Iran is considering using chemical weapons against its regional adversaries, a claim that has sparked sharply divided reactions among American officials, The New York Times reported Tuesday. While some officials expressed alarm, others reportedly viewed the intelligence with deep skepticism, questioning whether the warnings were intended to encourage renewed U.S. military action against Tehran. According to the report, some officials in Washington believe Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is attempting to persuade the Trump administration to resume major combat operations against Iran. Others consider the threat credible, particularly following recent intelligence warnings about possible Iranian attacks on American interests. Israel also has shared its assessments with officials in Gulf countries, several of whom questioned their credibility. According to a regional official cited by the Times, Israeli representatives presented their conclusions without supplying supporting evidence, leaving some Gulf governments unconvinced that Tehran was seriously preparing a chemical attack. The newspaper also pointed to Netanyahu's precarious political position following last week's Israeli elections, which left him without a clear path to forming a government. Some analysts suggested that a security emergency could provide leverage to persuade opposition leaders to join his coalition. Over the past two weeks, Israeli intelligence officials have reportedly described the chemical weapons threat as more urgent than Iran's nuclear ambitions. They believe Tehran is accelerating efforts to develop capabilities to deploy chemical agents through ballistic missiles or smuggle them into another country for an attack. Delivery by drone is also considered possible. However, experts noted that effectively dispersing chemical agents from a missile presents significant technical challenges. Despite the warnings, Israel's Home Front Command has not undertaken unusual preparations for chemical warfare. Although emergency drills are taking place this week, chemical weapons scenarios have not been a major focus, and no widespread guidance has been issued to military personnel or civilians. The IDF declined to comment on the report. American intelligence agencies have monitored Iran's chemical weapons activities for decades. A 2024 U.S. intelligence assessment warned that Tehran was likely continuing research into chemical and biological agents for offensive purposes. Dana Stroul, a former senior Pentagon official responsible for Middle East policy, said Iran had accumulated chemical weapons components over more than two decades without deploying them, although an existential threat could potentially change that calculation. The White House declined to comment on the intelligence, while an American official said President Donald Trump would protect the United States and its allies against potential threats. The CIA also declined to comment, and Iran's UN mission did not respond to a request for comment. Netanyahu's office said Israel was closely monitoring threats from Iran and remained prepared to respond to any danger posed by the Iranian regime.
news.summary: Israeli intelligence has divided American officials, with some alarmed by Tehran's alleged preparations and others suspecting Netanyahu is trying to draw Trump back into war; Gulf governments have also questioned the claims; no special preparations on Israel's home front

news.title: Why a growing number of younger Americans are having strokes
news.text:
When Connecticut Democratic Sen. Chris Murphy was hospitalized this weekend after suffering a stroke, President Donald Trump told reporters he was “surprised” by the news. 

“I just heard about it inside, and he’s a pretty young guy, so I was a little surprised to hear it,” the president said. “No, nobody wants to have that.”

Murphy, who is 53, is younger than many stroke victims, with most of the dangerous medical events occurring in people older than 65, according to Stanford Medicine. Though strokes may occur at any age, the risk for strokes rises as we get older and, each year, strokes kill 140,000 of the close to 800,000 people who have them. 

But the rate of strokes has also been on the rise in younger Americans for decades. The latest federal research shows the number of adults under age 44 who have had a stroke rose nearly 16 percent over the last decade and a University of Cincinnati study published in September found stroke rates in younger adults living in the Midwest nearly doubled from 1993 to 2020. 

That uptick is particularly concerning because stroke at a younger age can lead to living with disability for decades. Fortunately, experts believe they know why they’ve seen this pattern, tracing the rise to the use of opioids as well as increased cardiovascular risk factors, including high blood pressure and obesity. 

“What we found is that young adults experiencing strokes increasingly have high blood pressure, diabetes, high cholesterol, obesity and smoking histories,” Aaron Shoskes, a neurologist at University of Utah Health’s Clinical Neurosciences Center, said in April. “So, in many cases, this isn’t coming out of nowhere.”

A stroke occurs when the blood supply to part of the brain is blocked or when a blood vessel in the brain bursts.

Obesity, a chronic accumulation of excess fat that increases the risk of health complications, can raise the risk of strokes by sending blood pressure skyrocketing. High blood pressure can lead to blood clots that cause stroke. 

Obesity is also a risk factor for developing diabetes, a chronic condition that affects the body’s ability to produce insulin, a hormone that regulates blood sugar. Diabetes can raise the risk for stroke by 1.5 times by leading to blood clots, too. Both diabetes and obesity are linked to cancer, which may also be playing a role, Shoskes said. 

Cancer can raise the risk of stroke by making blood prone to clotting and 2019 Penn State College of Medicine research found cancer more than doubles the risk of dying from a stroke.

“While it’s not the primary driver of the trend, it’s likely one of several contributing factors,” Shoskes said. 

Rates of obesity, have climbed 37 percent in the U.S. over the last 20 years, according to the American Heart Association. That’s partially thanks to an increasingly processed diet, with more foods containing bad fats and high sugar and salt content.

Certain forms of cancer are on the rise in younger adults in the U.S. and worldwide, including colorectal cancer, pancreatic, prostate, kidney and multiple myeloma, according to Harvard experts.

Doctors are still working to understand why, but believe obesity plays a part. 

People can lower their risk of having a stroke by reducing their risk for obesity, diabetes and cancer.

That means keeping blood pressure and blood sugar at normal levels, and staying at a healthy weight for your body through diet and exercise. 

Following an overnight fast, blood sugar readings under 100 milligrams of sugar per deciliter of blood are considered to be normal, while those above 126 milligrams suggest a patient may have prediabetes or diabetes, according to the American Heart Association.

Blood pressure readings that are less than 120 systolic and less than 80 diastolic are considered OK, the association also notes. Systolic readings measure the force in your arteries as your heart beats, while diastolic readings measure blood pressure during the pause between the heartbeats.

To keep levels low, people should aim for 30 minutes of exercise each day, including cardio such as running, cycling and strength training. 

Experts also recommend that people follow a heart healthy diet, like the Mediterranean diet. The diet features anti-inflammatory foods, including dark leafy greens and olive oil.

“These lifestyle changes may not sound exciting, but they are some of the most powerful ways to lower stroke risk,” Shoskes says.
news.summary: Some 140,000 Americans die from strokes annually in the US

news.title: Binance reveals hackers used fake job interviews, malicious code in $6.3bn heist
news.text:
Binance released on Tuesday a detailed investigation into the $6.3 billion hack of its cryptocurrency platform, showing how attackers used fake job interviews and malicious code to steal the funds.

The crypto exchange said it had replenished 98 per cent of the affected assets by drawing on its own funds, with the remaining amount involving little-traded currencies that are harder to acquire.

The attack, carried out over about four hours on Oct 29, was attributed by the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) to North Korea-affiliated hackers.

Pyongyang has denied the allegations, with the powerful sister of leader Kim Jong Un calling the claim “absurd rhetoric”.

Around $2.85bn of the stolen $6.34bn has been frozen, Binance said, meaning that the attackers could not use it or convert it to another currency.

Binance is the world’s largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes.

News of the hacking attack, which is thought to be the biggest ever crypto heist, caused the prices of most major cryptocurrencies to fall sharply.

According to Binance, attackers took their first steps towards the breach as early as June.

First, they targeted a platform engineer by getting them to download a virus-laden version of the widely-known programming software Homebrew.

Binance’s cybersecurity teams identified the malware and removed it, but the hackers had already had time to harvest information about the engineer and his colleagues.

In September, the attackers approached another Binance engineer through a legitimate job-search platform, offering him an interview for a position in a fictitious company.

After building trust with the subject through the sharing of social media photos and videos, they asked the engineer to download a test exercise as part of the interview process.

The exercise contained malware that deployed “sophisticated obfuscation and evasion techniques,” Binance said, including replacing a legitimate development tool component with a malicious version.

That malware was critical to the success of the attack, as it allowed the hackers to establish a connection with Binance’s internal systems.

On October 20, the attackers used the access they had gained and an internal AI tool to gain control over software used by two other engineers.

Nine days later, they triggered malicious code that initiated the attack.

Binance says outflows normalised as North Korea rejects US allegation

Asset outflows from Binance have normalised and the company was in “very strong financial health”, its co-CEO said.

The world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange, whose customers had withdrawn a net $4.72bn as of Monday after the financial heist, has also launched a campaign to stem outflows and woo new users.

“In the first 24 hours, there was a spike in terms of withdrawals, as can be expected. But after that … it’s pretty much normalised,” Richard Teng told a Hong Kong Fintech Week event on Tuesday.

“The company is in very strong financial health,” he said.

“This is something that we can cover. We are able to do so.”

The crypto exchange was seeing “hourly deposits exceed withdrawals”, Binance said in an X post earlier on Tuesday, adding that it reflected improving user activity and stabilising flows.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said on the weekend that North Korea was responsible for the theft of more than $6bn in crypto assets, a crime that sent shockwaves through the industry.

Kim Yo Jong, the influential sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, said the US allegations proved Washington remained hostile towards Pyongyang, according to a report on Tuesday by state news agency KCNA.

Pyongyang has not responded to US President Donald Trump’s overtures, made earlier this year, to resume summit diplomacy. In the wake of the US allegations, Kim Yo Jong said North Korea had “issues to reconsider” over what she called US hostility.

“The FBI is trying to brand the DPRK as a ‘cyber criminal state’, claiming that it obtained information that a hacking organisation ‘supported’ by the DPRK was involved in the incident,” KCNA quoted Kim Yo Jong as saying.

“But the US assertion is absurd rhetoric and nothing new,” said Kim, a ruling party official. DPRK is short for the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea.

“It is a grave political provocation against the DPRK that the US misleads international public opinion as if all the cyber crimes in different parts of the world are our deeds.”

Revenue stream

North Korea faces growing scrutiny over cryptocurrency theft, which analysts say is a key source of funds for its weapons programmes.

Cybersecurity experts say North Korean hackers are among the world’s most prolific crypto thieves and the proceeds help fund the country’s efforts to develop nuclear weapons and ballistic missiles capable of hitting the United States.

North Korea has stolen cryptocurrency worth $7.6bn this year, more than in any previous year, according to estimates by blockchain analytics firm Elliptic.

North Korea denies allegations linking it to cryptocurrency theft and other cybercrimes.

Analysts in Seoul said Pyongyang’s unusually swift response likely reflected concern that the allegation could lead to tighter efforts to disrupt revenue streams that North Korea is accused of using to finance its weapons.

“With sanctions already in place, cryptocurrency theft has become one of North Korea’s key channels for securing funds for regime maintenance and weapons development,” said Lim Eul-chul, a professor at Kyungnam University’s Institute for Far Eastern Studies.

Additional US measures targeting crypto wallets, laundering networks and cryptocurrency exchanges could choke off an important source of revenue, Lim said.

South Korea’s central bank estimated North Korea’s gross domestic product at 47.18 trillion won ($35.09bn) in 2025, meaning the Binance theft could be equivalent to about a sixth of its economic output.

Blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis estimated 89pc of crypto hack losses in 2026 were linked to North Korea, up from 15pc in 2021.

It said the average reported loss per hack rose from $50.65 million in 2021 to $185.65m in 2026.

“I guess you could call it big game hunting, where they’re targeting these larger exchanges that may take more time and more complexity to be able to do … but the payoff can be relatively large,” said Alec Zebrick, senior manager of Asia-Pacific Global Services at Chainalysis.

North Korea is one of the world’s most impoverished countries but has poured resources secured through illicit means and activities banned under UN Security Council resolutions into its missile and nuclear programmes.

Kim Yo Jong said North Korea would “reconsider” unspecified issues in light of the “very unpleasant US hostile attitude”, without elaborating.

North Korea has not publicly responded to Trump’s offers to resume summit diplomacy.

Binance withdrawals

Binance launched a campaign on Monday offering fee rebates, rewards to eligible users who rack up at least $10,000 in cumulative trading volume, as well as annual percentage rates of up to 10pc on certain yield-generating products.

The exchange’s “community appreciation campaign” will run through Nov 21, a post on its website showed.

Binance, which froze withdrawals for more than two days after the hack and then started allowing customers to withdraw again on Sunday morning in some assets, reopened withdrawals for more assets on Tuesday.

Since the resumption of withdrawals, Binance has seen net outflows amounting to around 3pc of the assets on its platform, it said on Monday, a relatively modest figure that analysts said suggested customer confidence had largely held up.

“The relatively contained price reaction suggests a degree of maturity and resilience,” said Maksym Repa, head of DeFi at Lombard, a Bitcoin finance protocol backed by Franklin Templeton.

“Investors appear to be distinguishing between a security failure at a centralised exchange and a problem with the Bitcoin network itself.”

news.title: Democrats Claim First Victory Amid Predictions of Blue Wave
news.text:
The U.S. territory of Guam gave Democrats looking to flip Congress their first glimmer of hope on Election Day. 

The Pacific island is fourteen hours ahead of New York, so the territory’s polls provide early results. 

According to the unofficial vote count on Tuesday afternoon, Democrats flipped Guam’s non-voting delegate seat in the House from red to blue. 

Democrat Alicia Garrido Limtiaco led with 51 percent, or more than 15,600 votes, to Republican delegate James Moylan’s 48.8 percent, or 14,900 votes, with all precincts reporting. 

Moylan has served as Guam’s at-large delegate in the House since January 2023. He won reelection in 2024 by nearly six points, meaning the landscape there has shifted roughly eight points in Democrats’ direction since then if Tuesday’s early results hold.

It comes as Democrats look to flip the House majority from red to blue in the 2026 midterms, with Donald Trump facing strong headwinds as voters sour on the president over higher prices and the war in Iran. 

While Guam, an island with a population of just over 170,000, has a non-voting delegate, Democrats would need to net just three seats to secure the House majority on Tuesday, and multiple forecasts indicate the odds are in their favor. 

While the unofficial results indicated Guam’s at-large seat would go blue on Election Day, the U.S. territory could have mixed results as the Republican candidate for governor took the lead in the territory. 

Republican gubernatorial candidate Tony Ada and his running mate, E.J. Calvo, led Democratic candidate Therese Terlaje and running mate Sabina Perez by just over 1,000 votes.

Its current Democratic Governor Lou Leon Guerrero was first elected in 2018 and won reelection in 2022 but is term-limited. 

President Donald Trump quickly seized on the governor’s race in the small territory on Tuesday afternoon in a Truth Social post. 

“Guam, which has always been considered strongly Democrat, just had an early call for a REPUBLICAN Victory in the top spot, Governor — Congratulations to Tony Ada! Also, the Republicans have the Majority in the State Senate. Wow, hopefully that’s an indication for things to come!” he wrote. 

The president did not acknowledge the early results showing a Democrat leading for Guam’s seat in the House.

news.title: Trump's Next Two Years On The Line As US Midterms Counting Day Arrives
news.text: More than 230 million eligible voters across the United States are heading to the polls as the country votes in the 2026 midterm elections. With polling underway, the attention will now move to the counting of ballots which could reshape the balance of power in Washington.The elections are being closely watched as a test of US President Donald Trump's leadership midway through his second term. Republicans currently control both chambers of Congress, but their majorities are narrow. Democrats are hoping to change that, with their eyes on key Senate races and all 435 seats in the House of Representatives.If they succeed, Trump could face greater resistance to his legislative agenda, along with tougher Congressional scrutiny of his administration.A voter fills out their ballot at the Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial Library on November 03, 2026 in Washington, DCPhoto Credit: AFPDemocrats Eye Seven Senate SeatsAll 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 of the 100 seats in the Senate are up for grabs. Of the Senate seats being contested, 22 are currently held by Republicans.Democrats are targeting these seven states in particular -- Michigan, Maine, Ohio, Kansas, Texas, Iowa and Alaska. Winning these races could put them in a position to take control of the Senate.US Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, Democrat from New York, votes at a polling location on Election Day during the midterm elections in New York City on November 3, 2026Photo Credit: AFPRecent pre-election polls released by The New York Times and Siena University show Democrats with an advantage over Republicans in nearly all seven battleground states.The numbers suggest a difficult contest for Republicans, although the final outcome will depend on how voters turn out on Election Day.The current numbers in Congress leave little room for Republicans to lose ground. In the House, Speaker Mike Johnson has 218 Republicans and one independent, Kevin Kiley of California, against 214 Democrats. Two seats are vacant.The Senate currently has 53 Republicans and 47 Democrats. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to take control.What A Democratic Win Could Mean For TrumpA change in control of either chamber would have major consequences for the White House.If Democrats win control of Congress, they could use their position to step up investigations into the Trump administration, scrutinise its decisions and put greater checks on the President's policies.It would also make it harder for Trump to push through his legislative agenda.However, losing control of Congress would not leave the President without powers. Trump would still be able to govern through executive orders, although these can be challenged and overturned by courts or reversed by a future administration.A Democratic victory would therefore change the political equation in Washington, even as Trump remains in the White House.When Will US Midterm Results Come In?With voting taking place across different time zones, the first major indications of the outcome will emerge as polling stations begin closing in the eastern United States.The first closures are expected early Wednesday morning in India. Polling will then wind down across the country, moving westwards, with the last voting locations in Alaska expected to close around 11:30 am IST.Counting will begin as polling stations shut and election officials start tabulating ballots. Preliminary results from the first major group of states could start coming in around 5:30 am IST on November 4.However, there is no common counting schedule across the United States. Each state follows its own rules for processing and counting votes, including ballots cast in person, through mail-in voting and during early voting.Some states allow officials to process mail-in ballots before Election Day, while others restrict when the process can begin. This means results will not come in at the same pace everywhere.The 2024 elections offer an example of how long the process can take. According to an Al Jazeera report, it took eight days after voting to establish which party would control the House of Representatives.READ | How Trump And His Administration May Interfere In US Midterm ElectionsMore Than 57 Million Ballots Already CastA large number of Americans have already voted before Election Day.According to the Associated Press, more than 57 million ballots had been cast across 47 states and Washington DC as of Monday. This is higher than the little under 44.5 million ballots recorded across 49 states and Washington DC at the same stage in the 2022 midterm elections.The early voting numbers will be another important indicator as officials begin counting ballots and the results start coming in.The newly elected US Congress is scheduled to convene on January 3, 2027.

news.title: DeSantis Breaks With Trump Day Before Midterm as Democrats Surge
news.text: Florida Republican Governor Ron DeSantis criticized several elements of President Donald Trump's second-term agenda on the eve of the midterms, arguing that the prolonged Iran conflict, higher gasoline prices and the administration's handling of immigration enforcement had contributed to a difficult political environment for the GOP. In an interview with Stephen A. Smith on his podcast Straight Shooter, the term-limited governor said Democrats had "more momentum" heading into Tuesday's elections and claimed Republican campaigns and committees were seeing some of the same warning signs reflected in public polling. "The polls you're seeing that show the Democrats making potentially big gains, those numbers are the same that Republican campaigns are getting right now, Republican committees," DeSantis said. "When you're in a midterm cycle, it tends to go against the party in power. I think we're seeing some of those headwinds." DeSantis argued that Republicans were confronting voter dissatisfaction over inflation, gasoline prices and the Iran conflict. "Our candidates are running into the wind on that," he said. "And the Democrats have more momentum." Election Forecasts Final forecasts of the midterms have pointed to a “blue wave” for the Democratic Party. Historically, the party in the White House loses seats in the midterms, so Democrats have been optimistic about their chances to flip control of Congress. That optimism has grown as Trump’s approval rating has fallen amid voter frustration with the state of the economy and cost of living. Polls have given Democrats an edge in the battle to control the U.S. House of Representatives, as well as in key U.S. Senate races. As of Monday, RealClearPolitics gave Democrats an 8.9-point lead on the generic ballot. Nate Silver is bullish on Democrats’ chances to win the Senate. His polling aggregate gave them an edge in Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, North Carolina, Ohio and Texas, while pointing to very close races in Louisiana, Nebraska and South Carolina. On the generic ballot, his forecast gave Democrats a 9.4-point lead, which would be the largest for either party in the national popular vote since 2010. The last forecast by Elliott Morris' FiftyPlusOne model gave Democrats a 99 percent chance of winning the House, a 79 percent chance of flipping the Senate and a 79 percent chance of securing both the Senate and House. Natalie Baldassarre, the national press secretary for the Republican National Committee, told Newsweek on Monday that polls historically “underestimate support for Republicans.” “Polls may suggest one thing, but the American people get the final say, and Republicans remain laser-focused on driving voters to the polls, defying history, and protecting our majorities,” she said. GOP's Donalds, Moody Lead in Latest Florida Polling The comments from DeSantis, who unsuccessfully challenged Trump for the 2024 Republican presidential nomination, come as he prepares to leave office and speculation continues about whether he could make another White House bid in 2028. Republicans, meanwhile, face a competitive political environment in Florida, a state that has moved sharply toward the GOP in recent elections. Republican Representative Byron Donalds and former GOP Representative turned Democrat David Jolly won their parties' nominations to succeed DeSantis. And in the state's U.S. Senate race, GOP Senator Ashley Moody and Democratic state Representative Angie Nixon are running against each other. Nixon won her Democratic primary with 55.2 percent of the vote at the time the race was called. The political environment is a significant change from the previous presidential election. Trump carried Florida by 13.1 percentage points in 2024, representing a shift of 9.7 points to the right compared with the 2020 presidential election. Recent polling shows Republicans maintaining an advantage in Florida’s governor and Senate races. A New York Times/Siena University that was released on October 28 found Donalds leading Jolly 48 percent to 44 percent, while an October 19 YouGov/Univision survey put Donalds ahead 50 percent to 42 percent. Together, the surveys show Donalds leading by between 4 and 8 percentage points in the closing weeks of the race. For the Senate race, the Times/Siena poll put Moody ahead of Nixon 50 percent to 44 percent. An InsiderAdvantage poll that was conducted between October 28-29 showed Moody leading Nixon (49 percent to 43 percent). Newsweek reached out to the White House Tuesday for comment. DeSantis Warns Republicans About Florida DeSantis said Democrats were trying to turn the gubernatorial contest between Donalds and Jolly into a referendum on Trump. "What the Democrats are doing in Florida, what they are doing is they're just saying, 'Donalds has voted with Trump, Donald Trump, Donald Trump,'" DeSantis said. He acknowledged that such a strategy could be risky given the president's strength in the Sunshine State, but said Democrats were betting that dissatisfaction with Trump could hurt Donalds. DeSantis said he was particularly concerned about an enthusiasm gap between the parties, arguing that Democrats were turning out at a stronger rate while Republican voters were less energized than in recent elections. "The atmospherics are different now," he said. "Democrats are energized. Our voters are not as energized." DeSantis nevertheless said Republican candidates retained an advantage and argued that a large number of reliable GOP voters were still likely to cast ballots. However, he warned Republicans not to assume Florida's political transformation would be permanent. The governor pointed to voters who have switched their registration from Democratic or independent to Republican in recent years, arguing that the GOP still needed to earn their support. "It isn't like you're a Republican from the grave and would never vote for Democrat," DeSantis said. "So those are people you got to work to keep in the party." Prediction markets also continued to favor Republicans in Florida on Election Day. Kalshi gave Donalds a 66 percent chance of winning the governor’s race, compared with 34 percent for Jolly. Polymarket similarly put Donalds at 66 percent in the governor’s race. In the Senate contest, it gave Moody a 90 percent chance of winning, compared with 11 percent for Nixon. Prediction-market prices fluctuate and reflect traders’ expectations rather than polling of voters. DeSantis Breaks With Trump on Iran DeSantis' sharpest criticism of Trump came over the Iran war, which the governor described as a "big, big drag" on Republicans. He argued that some voters who supported Trump because of his opposition to prolonged American involvement in Middle Eastern conflicts had become disillusioned. "We have some of our voters who've checked out because they're like, 'I didn't want any more Middle East wars, and now we're doing it,'" DeSantis said. He said the political consequences might have been different if the conflict had ended quickly. Instead, he blamed the prolonged conflict for higher gasoline prices, an economic pressure that he argued voters encounter directly. "Gas is higher. It hurts people, working class people, and it's higher because of this conflict," DeSantis said. "That's just the fact. If you can't admit that to voters, then you're gaslighting them and they're not going to listen to you on other things." DeSantis warned that the political damage could continue well beyond the midterms if the conflict remained unresolved. "If it drags on for the rest of his presidency, it's going to be devastating to his ability to get anything done," he said. "And it is going to be very, very difficult for Republicans in the next cycle." DeSantis Calls Kristi Noem Appointment a 'Mistake' DeSantis also offered a pointed criticism of the Trump administration's approach to immigration enforcement, singling out former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem. "I just think having Kristi Noem be the secretary was a mistake," DeSantis said. His criticism was not directed at the administration's broader objective of enforcing immigration law, which he said he supported. Instead, DeSantis argued that the implementation of the policy had created unnecessary confrontations. "She wanted these conflicts," he said of Noem. "I think she wanted because it created news and created conflict. That's not the way you do it." Noem was fired as DHS secretary by Trump in March after a turbulent tenure marked by controversy over the administration’s immigration enforcement, including several deaths of civilians at the hands of federal agents, and a $220 million advertising campaign featuring Noem. Her departure followed congressional hearings in which she faced criticism from lawmakers in both parties. She was replaced with Markwayne Mullin by the president. Noem later served as a special envoy for the Shield of the Americas initiative. That envoy status ended in September, and she subsequently became a senior adviser to Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau, continuing work on the initiative. DeSantis contrasted the administration's approach with policies in Florida, where he said local law enforcement authorities cooperate with federal officials when they encounter people accused of crimes who are also in the country illegally. "I think the public still wants the law enforced, and many Latinos do, by the way," DeSantis said. "But I think that was unnecessary in terms of how that happened." 'Only Trump Can Pull That Off' Despite his criticisms, DeSantis made clear that he believes Republicans should preserve some of the political and policy priorities that Trump brought to the party. He cited immigration, prioritizing American workers and confronting China among the issues on which he believes Republicans should build on Trump's approach. "The core things that Trump came on the scene with, I think those are things you need to build on," DeSantis said. But he argued that other Republicans should not attempt to imitate Trump's political persona. "Only Trump can pull that off," he said. "You just got to be yourself. You're never going to be him. He is one of one." That distinction could become increasingly important as Republicans begin looking toward the 2028 presidential election and deciding how closely the party's next nominee should resemble Trump. DeSantis Revisits Failed 2024 Run When Smith raised the prospect of another presidential campaign, DeSantis did not rule out running again. Instead, he offered a candid assessment of why his 2024 campaign failed. DeSantis said that he believed the election presented Republicans with an unusually favorable opportunity and that Trump's grip on Republican primary voters proved difficult to overcome. "I just ran into a brick wall," DeSantis said. He recalled meeting Republican voters who told him they believed he could be a better president than Trump but nevertheless intended to support the president. DeSantis also argued that Trump's legal troubles during the campaign strengthened his support among Republican primary voters. "They kept indicting him and he got more popular," DeSantis said. "I'm sitting there praying, don't indict him. Don't indict him because I know he's got to get more popular." DeSantis ultimately ended his presidential campaign and endorsed Trump. DeSantis, 48, would be 50 when the next president takes office in January 2029, leaving him young enough to mount another presidential campaign in 2028 or potentially in later election cycles. DeSantis Looks Toward 2028 DeSantis did not announce another presidential campaign in the interview, but he openly discussed the strategic choices Republicans could confront in 2028. "Will '28 be a continuation election where they want another term effectively of Trump, or is it going to be a change election?" he said. "If it's a change election, the public wants change. Republicans can offer it." DeSantis suggested that a future Republican nominee could retain what he considers the successes of the Trump presidency while departing from the president on other issues. "We're going to take the successes that Trump had, build off them," he said. "But guess what. We're also going to do A, B and C." The immediate test, however, comes in Tuesday's midterms. DeSantis said Republicans still had advantages in Florida, but his assessment of the national environment was notably more pessimistic. "We're seeing it in Florida," he said. "You're seeing it in some of these other places. So this is a tough environment." Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors for this story: Jason Lemon and Anthony Murray.
news.summary: The GOP governor said he was particularly concerned about an enthusiasm gap between the parties.
