news.title: America votes: Democrats hope for midterm 'blue wave' as Trump faces test of his presidency
news.text: In-person voting is underway Tuesday in the U.S. midterm elections, widely seen as a referendum on President Donald Trump's second term. With his approval ratings at a low point, Democrats are hoping to capture both chambers of Congress - the House of Representatives and the Senate - whcih would make it much harder for the president to advance his agenda during his remaining two years in office and strengthening their position ahead of the 2028 presidential election. The first polling stations on the U.S. East Coast opened at noon Israel time, with voting beginning later in the day across the central and western United States. Even before Election Day, more than 57 million Americans had cast ballots through early in-person voting or by mail. That represents a significant increase from the 45 million who voted early in the 2022 midterms and offers an encouraging sign for Democrats, who hope frustration with Trump's policies, particularly the war in Iran and the resulting surge in gasoline prices, will drive large numbers of their supporters to the polls. Nevertheless, the outcome could still change significantly during Election Day itself, when Republicans traditionally account for a larger share of votes than they do during early voting. The first results are expected to begin arriving at 1 a.m. Wednesday Israel time, when polling stations close in parts of Indiana and Kentucky. The final polls will close in Alaska at 8 a.m. Israel time. An initial picture of the balance of power in Congress could emerge overnight or Wednesday morning. However, close races, particularly in states where counting mail-in ballots takes longer, may not be decided for several days. Polls point to a 'blue wave,' but Republicans could still surprise Midterm elections take place every four years, halfway through a president's term. Americans vote for representatives to numerous federal and state offices, including Congress, state legislatures, governorships and attorneys general. The elections are widely regarded as a referendum on the sitting president's performance, and historically, the president's party tends to lose ground. An initial picture of the balance of power in Congress could emerge overnight or Wednesday morning. However, close races, particularly in states where counting mail-in ballots takes longer, may not be decided for several days. The greatest attention is focused on the races for the Senate and House of Representatives. When the president's party controls both chambers, it is easier for the administration to advance legislation and policy initiatives. When the opposing party holds a majority, the president's ability to govern is significantly constrained, potentially turning him into a "lame duck." Republicans enter the elections holding majorities in both chambers. In the outgoing House, they have 218 seats compared with 214 for Democrats. Another lawmaker identifies as an independent but leans Republican, while two seats are vacant. In the Senate, Republicans hold a stronger 53-47 majority and can afford to lose up to three seats. In the event of a 50-50 tie, Vice President JD Vance would cast the deciding vote. But the Republican Party enters Election Day under considerable pressure. For months, polls have suggested that Democrats could regain control of the House. Since gasoline prices surged following the war in Iran, polling has also indicated a more competitive battle for the Senate. With a Democratic takeover of the House widely anticipated in pre-election assessments, much of the attention Tuesday night will focus on the closely contested Senate races. Thirty-five Senate seats are up for election, but only a handful of races are considered truly competitive. Their outcomes will determine control of the upper chamber. Polling on the eve of the vote showed unexpectedly close races in deeply conservative states that Trump carried by double-digit margins against Kamala Harris two years ago, including Alaska, Iowa, Ohio and South Carolina. Competitive contests are also unfolding in Texas, a major Republican stronghold that has not elected a Democrat to the Senate in 38 years, and Kansas, where Democrats have not won a Senate seat in 94 years. Some recent polls gave Democratic candidates substantial leads in several of these races. However, pollsters have warned that conservative voters in rural areas can be difficult to reach and that surveys may once again be underestimating Republican support. Others point out that polls underestimated Democratic strength in the previous midterm elections. Democrats are hoping that a surge in support from independent voters and moderate Republicans will produce a sweeping "blue wave," allowing them to capture both chambers of Congress simultaneously. Such an outcome has occurred in only three previous midterm elections, most recently 20 years ago, when public frustration over the Iraq war helped Democrats make major gains. In an effort to preserve Republican control of at least the Senate, Trump spent the past month holding a series of campaign rallies designed to energize his supporters and drive turnout. Many of those rallies took place in conservative states he won comfortably two years ago, reflecting the defensive position in which his party now finds itself. One of his central messages was a warning that the "radical left" could seize control of Washington, both now and in 2028. He argued that Democrats could then entrench their power for generations by appointing new Supreme Court justices and granting statehood to Washington, DC, and Puerto Rico, changes he said would give Democrats an advantage in the Senate. Israel at the center of Trump's 'election surprise' With gasoline prices and inflation still high, however, Trump's warnings about Democratic control have struggled to gain traction. The president has done little to help Republicans on that front, frequently appearing dismissive of Americans' economic difficulties. He has repeatedly described the surge in gasoline prices as a "small price" to pay for preventing Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons. Trump has also insisted that the economy is performing exceptionally well. In an interview with Fox News on Tuesday afternoon, he claimed that "inflation has been solved," even though annual inflation is expected to reach approximately 3.7% this year, well above the Federal Reserve's 2% target. Israel has also become a major issue in the elections, with American support for the country declining sharply following the wars in Gaza and Iran. In Michigan, for example, a close Senate race is underway between progressive Muslim Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, who has emphasized his opposition to continued US military assistance to Israel, and pro-Israel Republican Mike Rogers. Perhaps in an attempt to help the Republican candidate, Trump made a surprise announcement during his Fox News interview Tuesday, claiming that he had reached an agreement with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to end approximately $4 billion in annual US military aid to Israel. During the interview, Trump appeared to address arguments made by Democrats such as El-Sayed, who have criticized the assistance as a burden on American taxpayers, even though the funds are used to purchase U.S.-made weapons and military equipment. "The left uses the $4 billion payment, which everybody knows about and is no secret, to portray it as a symbol of unfairness, and we can't allow that to happen," Trump said. CNN suggested Tuesday evening that Trump's announcement was directly connected to the Michigan race. The president's campaign account on X later amplified the statement, posting an image with a large headline announcing the end of aid to Israel alongside the words "America First." Earlier, CNN reported, citing a White House source, that Trump had been optimistic during the initial stages of the campaign about Republicans' chances of defying expectations Tuesday night, but had grown more pessimistic in recent days, leaving him in a subdued mood. Later, however, CNN quoted a presidential adviser who insisted that Trump was in "great spirits." The adviser said the White House remained "cautiously optimistic." 'It's scary. We need change': Michigan voters voice frustration For many Americans, Tuesday's elections offer an opportunity to express dissatisfaction with Trump's policies. Beyond the unpopular war in Iran, the president has launched a mass deportation campaign against undocumented immigrants, which has sparked widespread anger and unrest in American cities. His administration has imposed tariffs on numerous countries, is engaged in a trade war with Canada and has pursued legal action against political opponents. "I feel I have a duty to do everything I can to change the direction our country is heading right now, to put it back on the path of democracy and away from autocracy," said Jane Callum, a 77-year-old retired teacher who voted for Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff in an Atlanta suburb. Georgia is considered a swing state, and Ossoff won his seat by a narrow margin six years ago. This time, amid frustration with Trump, polls show him holding a substantial lead over his Republican opponent, and the race is no longer considered competitive. In Macomb, Michigan, north of Detroit, 62-year-old voter Arnes Rogers told CNN he was hoping for change. "It's never been this bad. Gas prices are high. The economy is terrible. We've been losing jobs for the past two years, since he took office," he said. "I hope my company, one of the Big Three US automakers, can keep operating because our parts come from Canada. He's picking fights with everybody, and it's terrible to see where things are going in America right now. It's just scary." Another voter, Hayden Mendez, said he had cast his ballot for Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan. Alongside his criticism of Israel, El-Sayed has focused his campaign on the cost of living and health care. Mendez also cited the war in Iran as one of the reasons behind his decision. "I just think things never should have gotten this bad in the first place," he said. "But I hope whoever wins today actually looks out for the American people and chooses to do things that serve Americans instead of just making things worse for them." Election fraud fears and questions over whether Trump will accept the results Tuesday's elections are also taking place amid concerns that Trump, who continues to refuse to acknowledge his defeat to Joe Biden in the 2020 presidential election and has repeatedly made unsubstantiated claims of widespread voter fraud, could attempt to challenge or obstruct the midterm results. In recent months, Trump has raised numerous allegations of election fraud, while the federal administration has taken several steps that have alarmed election officials across the United States. California Gov. Gavin Newsom warned over the weekend that the Trump administration might attempt to seize ballots and other election materials, allegedly to interfere with the vote-counting process. 1,000 election monitors deployed, but no immigration agents near polling places On Monday night, the administration filed an emergency petition with the Supreme Court demanding that approximately 20,000 mail-in ballots in California be separated from the count until the eligibility of the voters could be established. The administration claimed that some of those voters might not be US citizens. California authorities countered that the list submitted by the federal government was unreliable and contained numerous errors. The Supreme Court quickly rejected the request. Another federal court challenge, filed last month, sought to prevent recognition of a possible defeat by Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska. The administration argued that a "spoiler candidate" with the same name as the senator was running in the race and could confuse voters. Trump claimed the candidacy amounted to "election fraud of the highest order," but the court rejected the petition. Asked last week whether he would accept the midterm election results, Trump offered only a conditional response: "I'll accept them if they're fair." The U.S. Justice Department also announced Tuesday that it had deployed 1,000 election monitors to polling locations across the country, primarily in Democratic strongholds, to ensure that voting procedures were conducted properly. More dramatic measures feared by Democrats, including the possible deployment of immigration enforcement agents or National Guard troops near polling stations to allegedly intimidate voters, have not materialized.
news.summary: More than 57 million Americans cast early ballots as Democrats seek control of both houses of Congress amid frustration over the Iran war, high gas prices and inflation;  first results are expected to begin arriving at 1 a.m. Wednesday Israel time

news.title: Trump celebrates early Republican gains in Guam, says ‘hopefully that’s an indication’ for US midterms
news.text: US President Donald Trump has welcomed Republican gains in Guam's gubernatorial election, congratulating Republican candidate Tony Ada and suggesting the result could signal wider gains for his party in the November 3 US midterm elections.“Guam, which has always been considered strongly Democrat, just had an early call for a REPUBLICAN Victory in the top spot, Governor — Congratulations to Tony Ada!” Trump wrote in a post on his Truth Social platform.He also claimed that Republicans had secured a majority in Guam's legislature and added: “Wow, hopefully that’s an indication for things to come!”According to the unofficial tally reported by local media, Ada and Calvo received 15,945 votes, or 51.45%, against 14,925 votes, or 48.15%, for Terlaje and Perez. The results are subject to certification by the Guam Election Commission.The Republican's unofficial victory came alongside another significant development for the party in Guam's local politics. Republicans secured eight of the 15 seats in the territory's legislature, compared with seven won by Democrats, according to Public Radio Guam. Democrats flip Guam's congressional seat: Unofficial resultThe gubernatorial gain was not the only major outcome of the election. Democrat Alicia Limtiaco defeated Republican incumbent James Moylan in the contest for Guam's delegate to the US House of Representatives.Limtiaco, a former attorney general of Guam, received 15,645 votes, or 51%, compared with Moylan's 14,983 votes, or 48.84%, according to the final unofficial tally reported by The Wall Street Journal.Moylan had won the seat in 2024 with 52.7% of the vote. Limtiaco's lead therefore represents a Democratic gain in the territory's congressional representation.However, Guam's delegate to the House does not have a vote on final passage of legislation on the House floor. The seat does not affect the balance of power between Republicans and Democrats in the chamber.Phillip Tydingco also defeated incumbent attorney general Doug Moylan in another key contest, according to Public Radio Guam.Why the Guam result mattersGuam is an unincorporated US territory in the western Pacific. Its residents are US citizens but cannot vote in the US presidential general election. They elect their own governor and a delegate to the US House, who can participate in House proceedings but cannot vote on final passage of legislation.The territory has a 15-member unicameral legislature, whose members are commonly called senators. Therefore, Trump's reference to a Republican majority in the "State Senate" was referring to the Republican majority in Guam's territorial legislature, not a separate state Senate.The outgoing governor, Democrat Lou Leon Guerrero, was term-limited and could not seek another term. Ada's victory ends the Democrats' eight-year hold on the governorship.The election produced a mixed outcome: Republicans won the governorship and a legislative majority, while Democrats captured Guam's congressional delegate seat.The Guam Election Commission's results remain unofficial. news.title: Fox News Viewer Numbers Drop Off—Here’s What They’re Watching Instead
news.text: Fox News, the most-watched cable network in America, lost 27 percent of its total day viewers in October compared with a year earlier, and its total day audience among adults aged 25-54 fell 32 percent to an average of 98,000 viewers, the lowest monthly level in 25 years, according to data from Nielsen. In widely reported remarks on an earning call on Monday, Lachlan Murdoch, the CEO of Fox News, said: “What we are seeing is some viewer fatigue, where our viewers have gone through an incredible news cycle last year with the inauguration, the Charlie Kirk tragedy, DOGE, flooding." “Those viewers are not switching to another news channel; they are just fatigued and watching slightly less television overall. We have seen this playbook, and we know how to move through it,” he said. There has been some evidence of a broader audience pullback from traditional news, with a December 2025 study from the Pew Research Center finding that the number of Americans who said they follow the news all or most of the time has decreased since 2016. Thirty-six percent of adults said they followed the news all or most of the time in August 2025, compared to 51 percent in 2016, per the Pew study. Meanwhile, the Reuters Institute’s 2026 Digital News Report found that 45 percent of Americans sometimes or often avoid the news. Despite the decline, Fox remains the dominant cable-news network in the country. It was the only cable network to average more than 1 million total-day viewers, ahead of ESPN despite the return of football and according to data from Nielsen, Comscore and Emplifi, Fox News accounted for 99 of the 100 highest-rated cable news telecasts during the month and is on pace for its highest-rated midterm election year in its 30-year history. The network also leverages 3.9 billion YouTube video views year-to-date, nearly 1 billion more than its closest cable news competitor. But the shift, ahead of the pivotal midterm election and as the network has had a slight change in tone on President Donald Trump, begs the question of what Fox News viewers are watching instead. Newsweek has reached out to Fox News’ press team for comment. Where Are Viewers Tuning in to? While no other network has the same dominance as Fox News, there is some data reflecting where viewers may be turning. And it appears that individual media personalities are the force drawing viewers. According to an analysis from Media Matters, the following six right-leaning shows that cover news and politics have seen subscriber growth on YouTube in recent months: Brandon Tatum's The Officer Tatum Show, Jeremy Hambly's The Quartering, The Colion Noir Podcast, Keeping It Real with Jillian Michaels, The Tim Dillon Show and Matt Fradd's Pints with Aquinas. From March through August, The Officer Tatum Show added 120,000 new subscribers and had 209 million views. The Quartering added 190,000 new subscribers through the same period and had nearly 96.3 million viewers. The Colion Noir added 100,000 new subscribers and had 86 million views, Keeping It Real with Jillian Michaels added 135,000 new subscribers and had more than 34.2 million views, Pints with Aquinas added 66,000 new subscribers and had more than 26.6 million views and The Tim Dillon Show added 170,000 new subscribers and had 34.8 million views. The same analysis identified three right-leaning news and politics shows that had an increase in viewership by tens of millions: The Glenn Beck Program, The Tucker Carlson Show and The Matt Walsh Show. During the same March through August period, The Glenn Beck Program had 83.9 million views and added 80,000 subscribers, The Tucker Carlson Show had 347.8 million views and added 260,000 subscribers and The Matt Walsh Show from the Daily Wire added 90,000 new subscribers and had nearly 96.6 million views. A similar personality-driven pattern was emerging earlier. Research from Edison Podcast Metrics, published in August that featured a review of audience numbers for conservative podcasts, captured audience increases over weekly consumers from the fourth quarter of 2024 and the second quarter of 2026. The Tucker Carlson Show was up 13 percent, and the Glenn Beck Program was up 11 percent. Other conservative shows, including the Megyn Kelly Show and the Shawn Ryan Show, had bigger boosts, up 115 percent and 107 percent, respectively. Has Fox News Changed Its Tone on Trump? Fox News has shown a subtle shift in its attitude toward Trump, carrying fewer of the president's appearances live, and covering some negative polls about the president's widely reported poor approval rating. That has drawn the ire of the president, who has regularly hit out at the network in recent weeks. “FoxNews spends more time covering the Jihadist and Dumocrat candidates than they do the good old fashioned Republicans, the people that have saved America, and are making it great again,” Trump wrote on Truth Social in early October. In September, he wrote on Truth Social: “MAGA, and REAL Patriots will never like Fox!” He criticized the network for giving airtime to Democrats, writing: “Why does FoxNews always put Chuck Schumer, Hakeem Jeffries, Jessica Tarlov, and every Democrat on, saying bad things about the Republican Party and, of course, me?” Fox News has previously seen fluctuations in its ratings that have hinged upon the mood among its viewership. In 2020, Fox News was criticized by Trump allies and the MAGA contingent after it accurately reported that Trump had lost to former President Joe Biden in 2024, which in turn put pressure on viewership. The network is still conservative in its core identity and has not become anti-Trump, but as the GOP begins to look ahead for what may come in 2028, it may be becoming less saturated. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Ben Kelly and Dave Siminoff.
news.summary: As Fox News acknowledges a viewership drop, data suggests there could be a personality-based pivot at play.

news.title: Kremlin Says Trump–Putin–Xi Meeting Could Be Finalized Within Days
news.text:
The Kremlin said on Nov. 3 that preparations were underway for a possible meeting between U.S. President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin, and Chinese leader Xi Jinping later this month, and expressed hope that arrangements could be finalized within days.

The three leaders could meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, scheduled for Nov. 18–19 in Shenzhen, China.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said there was a general understanding among the potential participants that such a meeting would be useful.

“We hope it will be finalized in the coming days,” Peskov told reporters, according to Interfax, a Russian news agency.

In a separate interview, Peskov said the three countries were exchanging diplomatic messages about their willingness to meet and discussing a possible agenda. He said China, as the host country, would take the lead in organizing the meeting.

“We would have it to talk about nuclear weapons and denuclearization,” Trump told reporters outside the White House. He said other subjects, including trade, could also be discussed.

On Oct. 28, Trump said he already had a meeting scheduled with Xi and that nuclear disarmament would be among the subjects discussed. He also expressed willingness to meet with Putin without Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy present, provided Ukraine was included in discussions about ending the war.

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier said he raised reports of a possible U.S.–Russia–China meeting on Ukraine directly with Xi during their Oct. 30 talks in Beijing.

In an interview with German public broadcaster ARD published Nov. 1, Steinmeier said Xi appeared surprised by the reports and rejected suggestions that a summit on Ukraine was being prepared.

According to Steinmeier, Xi said the three leaders would probably hold talks during the APEC summit, but that Ukraine was not intended to be the subject of those discussions.

Xi also said Europeans would need to participate in any negotiations over a peace settlement because the war was a European conflict, according to the German president.

Beijing’s official account of the Oct. 30 meeting confirmed that Xi and Steinmeier held talks but did not disclose their exchange about Ukraine or the possible three-way meeting.

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha had already objected to the proposed Trump–Putin–Xi meeting on the Ukraine war. On Oct. 19, he said talks involving Ukraine, Russia, and the United States could help end the war sooner, while replacing Ukraine with China would encourage Putin to continue fighting.

Separate negotiations on the Ukraine war are scheduled for Nov. 10–11 in Abu Dhabi, bringing together representatives of Russia, Ukraine, and the United States.

Peskov confirmed the dates on Nov. 3, saying Russia would send a delegation. The United States is expected to mediate the talks, which will address security guarantees and other issues related to ending the war.

Peskov said European representatives would not participate because the agreed format was limited to Russia and Ukraine, with U.S. mediation.
news.summary: German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier says Xi rejected the idea of a three-way summit focused on the Ukraine war.
news.author: Arthur Zhang

news.title: Trump declares ‘inflation is solved’ as Americans battling cost-of-living head to polls
news.text:
President Donald Trump declared that “inflation is solved” as many Americans head to the polls with the cost-of-living on their minds. 

Trump dialed into Fox News on Election Day morning to make the sweeping claim. “And the toughest job I was given, the inflation is solved,” he said Tuesday on Fox & Friends. “Everything’s going good… everybody respects us again.”

The latest inflation figures, released October 29, tell a different story. 

Consumer prices rose 3.6 percent in September from a year earlier, the U.S. Commerce Department said last week, up from 3.4 percent in August. On a monthly basis, prices climbed 0.5 percent, up from 0.3 percent in August — the highest figure since May. 

Nearly half of registered voters (48 percent) named cost-of-living as the top issue in deciding how they would vote, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll. The Federal Reserve’s inflation target is 2 percent, a rate not seen in nearly a decade.

Even conservative analysts called out the president over his inflation claim. 

“This is untrue,” Joel Griffith of Advancing American Freedom, a conservative group founded by Trump’s former VP Mike Pence, posted on X. “American families are losing ground as inflation is [sic] heats up.”

During a speech on election eve, Trump described the elections as “the most important midterm, I believe in our lifetime.” The president delivered the speech in front of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, where he spent the first 20 minutes talking about the renovation of the landmark, which was significantly delayed due to a botched repair of the lining.

Critics, including former Georgia congresswoman and ex-Trump-loyalist Marjorie Taylor Greene, called out the president for not using the opportunity to talk about the cost of living.

“So today for Trump’s closing midterm pitch he goes to the reflecting pool and brags all about working on the reflecting pool that 99.99999999999999% of Americans don’t care about and it has no effect on their lives like continued high inflation, high cost of living, high cost of gas/diesel does,” Greene posted on X.

After much criticism of the speech, Trump fumed Tuesday that the address “wasn't a Final Midterms Speech.”

“It was a NEWS CONFERENCE, nobody was invited, it was closed to the Public — Just Reporters,” he raged on Truth Social. “My Final Midterms Speech was the day before in lowa and Kansas, where we had 50,000 people. This just shows you how FAKE the News is.”

Trump campaigned for a second White House term on a promise to turbocharge the economy. But his presidential approval rating has fallen in recent months to the lowest levels of his political career, including among Hispanic Americans who swung in his direction in 2024.

According to the Reuters/Ipsos poll, 49 percent of Americans said their household finances have deteriorated since January 2025, when Trump returned to power, compared to 13 percent who said their finances had improved and 37 percent who said things were about the same.

With reporting from agencies
news.summary: Nearly half of registered voters named cost-of-living as the top issue in deciding how they would vote, according to one poll
news.author: Rhian Lubin

news.title: Opinion: Martha Stewart dressing up as a socioeconomic crisis was a perfect reflection of the times
news.text:
Like most children in the 1990s, my family’s fancy-dress costumes comprised whatever low-effort ensemble could be fashioned out of a black bin liner or a cardboard box. And so, for Halloween 1989, my dad decided that one of his eight children should go as the Berlin Wall. Communism may have been dead, but Halloween as a cultural reference point was just beginning. And okay, it was 1989, everybody except for a pissed off five-year-old (who had put a LOT of effort into her witchy bin-bag) “got” the significance of the Berlin Wall. 

In hindsight, this was a primitive version of “Gay Halloween”, a modern trend that thrives on dressing up as the most obscure cultural reference. Think Molly, the automaton bird that Kelly Clarkson recently tried and failed to buy, or Cynthia Erivo of Wicked’s acrylic nail. The costume is less about being scary (Erivo’s nails are terrifying, mind) and more about how fluent you are in the language of niche cultural allusions. Like memes and reels, costumes are now acts of visual quotation and interpretation, not really made to go to a party so much as shared on the internet. 

This year, Martha Stewart missed the memo and decided to dress as a socioeconomic crisis. If many Halloween costumes now thrive on obscure in-jokes, this was a bad stereotype. In the photo, which was shared to her Instagram account, Stewart stands before the Clapboard exterior of Cantitoe Corners, her 150-acre farm in Bedford, New York, like a modern-day Marie Antoinette cosplaying at peasant life. She’s dressed in a wealthy person’s approximation of Seattle grunge, dirt smeared across her face. She holds a clipboard that says “I am hungry! Help me!”. A giant Chow Chow stares down the lens, bewildered, while a small French bulldog regards his owner with distaste. The photo appeared in a reel promoting Stewart’s QVC candle collection and caused an outcry for its insensitivity. “Why do you think poor people who are dying on the side of the road are a costume?” one follower posted on Instagram. Stewart quickly removed the photo, but it continued to circulate online. 

The homemaker entrepreneur initially maintained that the costume had been social commentary and “was intended to bring more awareness to the very serious subject of homelessness”. “Homelessness continues to remain one of America’s greatest challenges and ongoing crises,” Stewart went on to say, “something that I care deeply about.” In a follow-up on Instagram, however, Stewart acknowledged that her initial statement had been inadequate. “It’s hard to admit when you’ve really screwed up,” she wrote to her 5.9 million followers. “I know many people are suffering economically. Wearing a costume like I did was insensitive and not funny. I am very sorry.”

The intention was beside the point. Today’s costumes are visual shorthand; they can invoke a whole set of cultural touchstones without voicing their argument. Sometimes the result is an elaborate in-joke. Sometimes it is a political statement. And sometimes, as with Stewart, the image says more than the maker probably intended. If Martha Stewart hoped to raise awareness, she drew attention to the extraordinary distance between those in the United States who experience poverty and those wealthy enough to cosplay it for Halloween. 

In the time since plastic bag witch costumes and the fall of communism, we’ve also seen an extraordinary expansion of politics conducted through images. 

Writing in the 1930s, the philosopher Walter Benjamin argued that film and photography transformed the relationship between images and politics. Images could be made and shared widely, offering new possibilities for political expression. Benjamin was thinking about the aesthetics of fascism like the Nuremberg rallies. But everyday people would be able to express themselves this way too, without necessarily having the power to change their material circumstances. It’s a distinction that lands today. So much politics happens through the shorthand of an image – a tradwife dressed in cottagecore, a rich American cosplaying as a poor American, a president dressed as a McDonald’s worker.

Think of October 30th 2024, when Donald Trump donned a high-vis vest and climbed into a garbage truck in response to comments from Biden that his supporters were trash. Politics is no longer about coherent narratives, so much as visual spectacle. This Halloween, Trump – who understands how to create a spectacle better than anyone – hosted a lavish pre-midterm party at Mar-a-Lago and came in the most elaborate costume of all: he dressed as himself.
news.summary: Politics is no longer about coherent narratives so much as visual spectacle
news.author: Rachel O'dwyer

news.title: Kennedy Center names Anka, Garcia among 2026 honorees | Kuwait Times Newspaper
news.text:
The Kennedy Center, the famed Washington arts hub that President Donald Trump has sought to overhaul, on Monday named singer Paul Anka and actor Andy Garcia among five honorees recognized for lifetime artist contributions. Composer and producer David Foster, playwright David Mamet and musician Barbara Mandrell were also listed as recipients of the Kennedy Center Honors, one of the United States’ highest arts awards. This year’s ceremony will for the first time be hosted at Washington’s Capital One Arena rather than the Kennedy Center, which has been shuttered since September amid a legal battle over renovations. Trump hosted last year’s awards program, which included “Rocky” actor Sylvester Stallone, country singer George Strait, disco legend Gloria Gaynor and rock band KISS.

The Kennedy Center had long enjoyed bipartisan support before Trump appointed himself board chairman in February 2025, pledging to end “woke political programming” at the site. A host of artists canceled concerts at the venue in response to Trump’s takeover, while US media has reported that Kennedy Center ticket sales have plummeted. — AFP

news.title: Tasha Kheiriddin: Everyone’s looking for a handout from this week’s budget. Can Carney resist?
news.text:
With Americans heading to the polls for their midterm elections, it feels like Thursday’s federal budget is getting a lot less media attention than usual. Ottawa might not mind this: every time U.S. President Donald Trump twitches, Prime Minister Mark Carney’s popularity rises. But while Washington commands the headlines, Canadians should check out the creeping sea of red ink below the fold — and just what it is funding.

Last year’s budget saw Ottawa rack up the biggest non-pandemic budget deficit in history, a whopping $80 billion; this year it is projected to top $63 billion. And while the government claims it will return its operating budget to balance in 2028-29, a revival of corporate welfare policies of governments past, repackaged as nation-building, promises big overall deficits for years to come.

Consider last week’s announcement of up to $1.6 billion in federal investment in the Canadian artificial intelligence company Cohere. The rationale is familiar: Canada must nurture domestic champions, retain intellectual property and compete with global technology giants.

Perhaps. But the move is already raising eyebrows about the cozy relationships between some of Cohere’s investors and the Liberal government. There’s also government’s failure to pick winners: consider the recent case of Northvolt, Quebec’s $650-million EV battery boondoggle or Ottawa’s long history of subsidies to Bombardier, which laid off employees nonetheless.

To his credit, Carney has also embraced less dirigiste approaches. His Productivity Mega Deduction, announced in September, would allow businesses to immediately write off a much broader range of capital investments. Ottawa estimates the measure will cost $36 billion over five years while reducing Canada’s marginal effective tax rate on new investments from approximately 13 per cent to 6.4 per cent — making Canada more tax-friendly than the United States.

Economically, that’s a better kind of industrial policy: rather than choosing corporate champions, government creates incentives for businesses across the economy to invest, innovate and compete, and makes us more competitive than other jurisdictions.

Politically, however, targeted spending remains irresistible. Billion-dollar announcements generate headlines and photo opportunities with workers and grateful corporate executives. Broad-based tax reform produces no ribbon-cuttings, even when its economic benefits are potentially much greater.

And with six byelections just called for December, three of which are in Quebec, watch for a lot of money to flow in an eastward direction. Already the French title of the budget, “Maitres Chez Nous” (“Masters of Our Destiny”), echoes the clarion cry of Jean Lesage’s government in the 1960s, when it established Hydro-Québec as a vehicle for Quebec’s economic development. The cover of the budget document even features an image of hydro lines soaring over Churchill Falls.

Meanwhile, business is also asking for tax relief. The Canadian Federation of Independent Business wants the small-business tax rate reduced from nine to six per cent and the deduction threshold increased from $500,000 to $700,000. Agricultural producers want changes to the tax code to smooth inter-generational transfers of family farms. The Canadian ETF Association wants Carney to create a “Maple Investment” tax-free savings account to incentivize investment in Canadian companies and is urging the government to bring back a pre-2022 taxation system for exchange-traded funds. 

Ordinary Canadians want help, too: at the grocery store, gas pump and in the housing market. Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre has called for an end to diesel taxes and spending restraint. The cost of living continues to be the top issue of concern, with a shocking one-third of Canadians saying they skip meals because they cannot afford groceries.

In Budget 2026, Carney faces a tough assignment: stimulating investment, helping struggling Canadians and satisfying the chorus of industries demanding tax relief. But borrowing more money to achieve these objectives isn’t the answer: it just kicks the can down the road for future generations, who already face a less prosperous future than the one before.
news.author: Tasha Kheiriddin

news.title: Trump Says US Ending Annual Aid to Israel, Amid Push for Military Integration
news.text:
On the morning of the critical midterm elections, President Donald Trump said that the U.S. is going to end its annual funding to Israel of roughly $4 billion a year starting in 2027 — a move Trump said was made at the direct request of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has been pushing for an even deeper, more secretive collaboration between the two countries.

Trump made the announcement on Fox and Friends on Tuesday morning, saying that the U.S.’s funding of Israel has become “too easy” of a target for critics and that the U.S. is going to continue the partnership in different ways. 

He said that Israel doesn’t “need” the aid, but that the U.S. will send them more if they need it and that Israel will still be able to “buy whatever they want” in terms of U.S. weapons. Israeli officials have not confirmed Trump’s announcement, and it’s unclear if it was just a last-second claim to boost Republicans at the polls.

“We made a deal months ago that we’re stopping, and they’re fine with it,” Trump said. “It gets cut off at the end of the year. Because they don’t need it. I asked them — they don’t need it.”

This does not mean that the U.S. is ending aid altogether, as Trump said. Rather, for years, the U.S. and Israel have been working on creating a new, deeper collaboration that is less subject to public disclosure and scrutiny — a project dubbed by backers as a “Special Relationship 2.0.”

“President Trump is a serial liar who has announced over $20 billion in weapons giveaways to Israel since taking office,” said Institute for Middle East Understanding Policy Project in a statement. 

The 10-year memorandum of understanding (MOU) between the U.S. and Israel to provide $3.8 billion in economic and military aid each year was already slated to expire in 2028. 

Negotiations have been ongoing for a new MOU, but Netanyahu and many pro-Israel advocates have been pushing instead for provisions like the unprecedented U.S.-Israel military integration measure that’s included in this year’s Pentagon funding bill. Under the new relationship, the focus would not be on aid, but partnership, collaboration, and full on combinations of U.S. military and technological industries.

Indeed, Trump said it was originally Netanyahu who approached him with the idea, which they have been discussing for “a couple of years.” 

“Can I be honest with you? He brought it up. He said, ‘I think it would be appropriate if we do not receive aid.’ Because he understands that this is one of their points of contention,” Trump said.

Trump also openly acknowledged that the reason for the change is purely to take away a line of attack against Republicans from left-wing critics as the Democratic Party undergoes a shift on Israel-Palestine. He said that the annual funding makes such criticisms “too easy.” 

“Why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like an [Abdul] El-Sayed when they don’t need it? It’s a bad talking point,” Trump said. “The left uses the $4 billion payment — that everybody knows about, it’s no secret — as a signal of unfairness, and we can’t allow that to happen.”

Notably, Trump didn’t address whether or not the U.S. would end its practice of providing Israel with billions of dollars’ worth of weapons on top of the annual funding. In the first two years of Israel’s genocide in Gaza, the U.S. provided a record $21.7 billion in military aid to Israel, according to Brown University’s Costs of War project, which notes that that estimate is highly conservative. Several more weapons transfers to Israel are currently pending, including a U.S. taxpayer-funded package of $3 billion worth of 2,000-pound bombs.

As critics of the U.S.-Israel partnership have been saying for months, the announcement is actually a long-term strategy by Israel to take the relationship one step further by hiding collaborations and military information-sharing behind classified Department of Defense operations. Such a change, advocates say, does not alter the pro-Palestine movement’s call for a full arms embargo, sanctions, and a boycott of Israel in order to end its genocide and occupation of Palestine. 

“He and other politicians realize our taxpayer funding for Israel is a liability,” the Institute for Middle East Understanding Policy Project said. “That’s why he and his allies in Congress are at this very moment trying to advance legislation to conceal support for Israel by integrating Israeli weapons companies into the Pentagon. This is a bait and switch that would result in Americans funding Israeli weapons makers in record amounts.”

Trump, meanwhile, spoke very fondly of his relationship with Israel and his high approval rating among its citizens. 

“If people ever get tired of me in the U.S., I’ll move to Israel and become prime minister,” he said.
news.summary: The US-Israel memorandum of understanding was already slated to end in 2028.
news.author: Sharon Zhang

news.title: USA Banned Government Agencies from Using Acronis Software, Developed by Natives of Russia
news.text:
Acronis, headquartered in Switzerland, develops software for data protection and recovery, backup, and secure file sharing. The company was founded in the early 2000s by graduates of the Moscow Institute of Physics and Technology. According to sources from Nextgov/FCW, American authorities have been checking it for possible ties to Russia and national security threats for almost ten years, since the first Donald Trump administration.

Both civilian and defense structures of the USA used Acronis software. Among them were the Pentagon's Defense Information Systems Agency, the Drug Enforcement Administration, and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. During inspections, American authorities, in particular, were finding out whether the company's employees in Russia continued to participate in the development of its products.

Acronis emerged in 2001 as a division of SWsoft, a company founded by graduates of the Moscow Institute of Physics and Technology (MIPT). Among them was Sergey Belousov, who left Russia in 1993 and later obtained Singaporean citizenship. American authorities previously suspected him of possible involvement in transferring classified information to Russian state structures.

According to CNews, Belousov's company historically relied heavily on Russian developers, a significant portion of whom worked in Russia for a long time. In addition, Acronis was for a long time one of the key residents of the MIPT technopark.

The company received large government contracts, including for Pentagon data backup. The Washington Post wrote about this in 2022. In 2021, Belousov himself changed his name to Serg Bell. After the start of the full-scale war against Ukraine, he condemned the Russian invasion.

At the same time, the Acronis-related company Acronis Infoprotection, now called "Cyberprotect," adapted and resold Acronis cybersecurity products to Russian state structures.

As Nextgov notes, as early as July 2025, the US banned the use of Acronis software in the networks of the American intelligence community, which unites 17 agencies, including the FBI and CIA. Later, a similar restriction was extended to the US Department of Defense.
